Why Iran’s hardliners keep talking of ousting Pezeshkian. Renewed talk among Iranian hardliners of removing President Masoud Pezeshkian has revived comparisons with Iran’s only presidential impeachment, but there is little evidence so far of a coordinated effort capable of unseating him.

Iran rapidly rebuilding site tied to past nuclear weapons research - report. Iran is rapidly reconstructing a heavily fortified facility at the Parchin military complex that was previously linked to nuclear weapons research and has been struck twice since 2024, new satellite imagery analyzed by a Washington-based nuclear watchdog shows.

US offers substantial whistleblower rewards for tips on Iran sanction evasion. The US Treasury is offering whistleblowers up to 30% of collected penalties for information leading to enforcement actions over Iran-related sanctions evasion or money laundering, as Washington seeks intelligence on Tehran’s financial networks abroad.

Trump weighs major Iran escalation as China steps up diplomatic push. President Donald Trump said Thursday he was weighing renewed large-scale strikes on Iran as China intensified diplomatic contacts with Washington and Tehran amid mounting pressure to contain the regional conflict.

Iran’s nightly pro-state rallies become factional battleground. Iran’s nightly pro-government rallies have become an increasingly visible show of political force, occupying streets and squares for 200 consecutive nights and, more recently, turning their fire on rivals within the Islamic Republic itself.

Iranian protester, 21, dies after about 30 operations for gunshot wounds. A 21-year-old taekwondo athlete shot by Iranian security forces during January protests has died after undergoing about 30 operations, according to information received by Iran International.

Iran faces postwar winter with a third of gas capacity lost. Iran is racing to restore gas infrastructure before winter after losing about a third of its pre-war production capacity, a reconstruction challenge that could force Tehran into difficult choices between keeping homes warm, power plants running and industry supplied.

Iran's Guards stage show of force two days after protest anniversary. Iran's Revolutionary Guards paraded uniformed volunteers, Basij paramilitaries and children through Tehran on Friday in a state-organized show of force, two days after the anniversary of the 2022 protests.

Tehran ‘ashamed’ as Iranians struggle to make ends meet. Iran’s economic hardship has grown so acute that senior government officials are increasingly acknowledging in public the scale of the pressure on ordinary households.

Unveiled runners draw attention at Tehran 10k race. Videos showing women running without headscarves at a road race in Tehran went viral on Friday, months after a similar event on Kish Island prompted action against its organizers.

Democrats seize on Iran war costs to hit Trump ahead of midterms. Democrats are intensifying attacks on President Donald Trump over the Iran war as the midterm elections approach, seeking to tie the six-month conflict to an issue closer to American voters’ wallets: the rising cost of gasoline and everyday goods.

Tehran sees ‌Beijing as potential bridge to Washington. Iranian officials and media are increasingly looking to China as a possible diplomatic bridge to Washington, as Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi’s second wartime visit to Beijing coincides with preparations for President Xi Jinping’s talks with Donald Trump next week.

Death-row Iran protester denied hospital treatment, family says. An Iranian woman sentenced to death over January’s anti-government protests is struggling to walk but has been denied hospital treatment despite a prison doctor saying she urgently needs an MRI, her family told Iran International.

Iran executes man it accused of spying for Israel on missile sites. Iran has executed a man it accused of passing information about missile sites in Isfahan to Israel's Mossad, the judiciary said on Saturday, the latest in a series of espionage executions that rights groups say rest on confessions extracted in detention.

Iran sets seven terms for renewed US talks, says ready for escalation. Iran has conveyed seven conditions to Washington for the start of any negotiations, Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Saturday, as President Donald Trump weighs whether to resume major attacks on Iran.

Will shutdowns forced by US blockade damage Iran’s oil wells?. The sharp fall in Iran’s oil loadings is forcing it to curb production, raising costs beyond lost sales, from restarting aging wells to maintaining reservoir pressure and protecting shared fields. But could the shutdowns cause lasting damage?

Iran mobilisation drive extends to children under 15. The spokesman for Iran’s mass mobilisation campaign said children under 15 could be introduced to military concepts, while denying that minors were receiving formal weapons training as authorities expand a civilian defence drive launched during the war.

Iran threatens regional strikes as MPs question nuclear policy. Iran’s military threatened sustained attacks on US bases and interests across the Middle East on Sunday, while parliament speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf argued that Tehran must both fight and negotiate.

How a Basij-linked cultural network helped identify Iran protesters. A local network tied to state-backed cultural and media groups helped Iranian authorities identify protesters during the January crackdown, with footage passed to Revolutionary Guards intelligence, sources familiar with the operation told Iran International.

Iran factories face deepening raw material shortages. Iranian manufacturers are rapidly running down stocks of raw materials as supply disruptions and rising costs deepen pressure on industrial production, according to the latest survey by the Iran Chamber of Commerce.

Trump weighs Iran options; Tehran signals Hormuz leverage. US President Donald Trump weighed military action, economic pressure and a possible deal with Iran, while Iranian leaders paired diplomatic overtures with warnings over the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.

Economic crisis puts Iran’s coal miners at greater risk. Iran’s economic crisis and rising currency costs are making essential safety equipment harder for coal mines to obtain, increasing risks for workers already operating in dangerous conditions, labor news agency ILNA reported on Monday.

Frozen embryos advertised for sale online in Iran. An informal market for frozen embryos appears to be emerging on Iranian social media and online marketplaces, where sellers are advertising them for cash outside the country’s donation system, local media reported on Monday.

Rwanda-Bénin : chez Paul Kagame, les dossiers très sécuritaires de Romuald Wadagni. Avant Brazzaville, où il est arrivé ce 17 septembre, le président béninois a effectué une visite officielle à Kigali. Au cœur des discussions avec son homologue rwandais, le renforcement du partenariat sur les questions militaires et de renseignements.

Côte d’Ivoire : la justice allège les charges contre Blaise Lasm, proche de Laurent Gbagbo. Détenu depuis septembre 2025, le responsable du PPA-CI a obtenu un non-lieu partiel. Son dossier est désormais renvoyé devant le tribunal correctionnel.

Cameroun : dans les coulisses d’un renseignement d’État privatisé. Officiellement destinés à protéger l’État, les services de renseignement du Cameroun, précarisés, se mettent régulièrement au service d’intérêts privés contre rémunération. Plongée au cœur du marché noir des informations.

Niger : dans la tête d’Abdourahamane Tiani, président retranché. Après la mutinerie du 29 août, le chef de la junte semble plus isolé que jamais. Il se méfie de son armée, et ne fait plus confiance qu’à sa Garde présidentielle, à une poignée d’officiers encore fidèles et à ses alliés russes et algériens.

Après l’Algérie, la Tunisie de Kaïs Saïed déclare la guerre au narcotrafic. Quelques jours après le voisin algérien, la Tunisie annonce à son tour vouloir renforcer la lutte contre les réseaux de trafic de stupéfiants. Dans les deux pays, les quantités saisies et la consommation ont explosé ces dernières années.

Au Maroc, l’héritage bénéfique de la crise de la BNDE. Après avoir servi de bras armé du royaume en matière de financement de l’industrie, la BNDE a été liquidée au milieu des années 2000 sur fond de scandale financier. Ce dossier a conduit à un renforcement de la régulation bancaire au Maroc.

Déguerpissements en Côte d’Ivoire : le gouverneur d’Abidjan, Ibrahim Cissé Bacongo, fragilisé. Les révélations du procureur sur le rôle d’Ibrahim Cissé Bacongo dans la destruction de 250 logements à Koumassi affaiblissent le secrétaire exécutif du parti présidentiel. Elles questionnent aussi l’encadrement de ces opérations de démolition qui se sont multipliées à Abidjan.

Finale de la Coupe du monde 2030 : face aux ambitions du Maroc, l’Espagne menace. Depuis l’attribution du tournoi 2030 au trio Maroc-Portugal-Espagne, la question de savoir quel pays accueillera la finale oppose Madrid et Rabat. Une rivalité envenimée par la crise de Ceuta et la dégradation de leurs relations diplomatiques.

Mark Suzman (Fondation Gates) : « L’IA peut permettre d’atteindre les objectifs de développement du continent ». Le PDG de la Fondation Gates alerte sur les conséquences de la baisse de l’aide publique au développement. Et parie sur l’intelligence artificielle pour lutter contre la pauvreté, les maladies et améliorer l’éducation.

Ambassades et liaisons aériennes : à New York, le Maroc et Israël renforcent leurs liens. Lors d’une rencontre à trois incluant l’ambassadeur américain aux Nations unies, les ministres marocain et israélien des Affaires étrangères ont notamment décidé de transformer leurs représentations diplomatiques en véritables ambassades.

Transport maritime : Hapag-Lloyd et DP World, la revanche africaine des outsiders. Le cinquième armateur mondial et l’opérateur portuaire émirati scellent une collaboration sur le long terme dans cinq ports africains, qui doit apporter un peu plus de visibilité au premier et de respectabilité au second.

Niger : qui sont les personnalités déchues de leur nationalité par Abdourahamane Tiani ?. Le chef de la junte a déchu provisoirement de leur nationalité cinq de ses compatriotes, parmi lesquels plusieurs anciens responsables du régime de Mohamed Bazoum. Une mesure qui intervient moins de trois semaines après les événements du 29 août à Niamey.

Les marchés de capitaux, grands gagnants de l’IPO Dangote. Avec l’entrée en Bourse de sa raffinerie, Dangote entend mettre les épargnants nigérians au cœur de l’essor industriel du pays. Mais l’opération teste aussi la capacité du Nigeria à faire de Lagos une place financière de premier plan.

Au Sénégal, Bassirou Diomaye Faye cultive le mystère autour des élections locales. La confusion règne autour du calendrier des élections municipales et départementales initialement prévues en janvier 2027, qui seront probablement reportées sans que Bassirou Diomaye Faye ne s’en soit jusqu’à présent expliqué. Alors qu’il ne bénéficie plus du soutien de Pastef, le chef de l’État appréhenderait-il cette confrontation électorale à haut risque au point de chercher à l’ajourner ?

En RDC, l’ancien ministre Constant Mutamba poursuit sa dégringolade. Déjà condamné à trois ans de travaux forcés, en septembre 2025, l’ex-ministre de la Justice a été reconnu coupable de détournement de fonds destinés à l’indemnisation des victimes de la guerre de Kisangani. Il écope cette fois d’une peine de dix ans de prison et poursuit sa chute spectaculaire, un an après sa démission du gouvernement.

Guerre des drones au Mali, interview exclusive de Fouzi Lekjaâ, les secrets du renseignement camerounais… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique enquête sur les victimes civiles des frappes de drones au Mali, revient sur les ambitions politiques de Fouzi Lekjaâ au Maroc, dévoile les dessous de la guerre des clans qui fragilise les services de renseignements camerounais, décrypte les affrontements entre opposition et partisans du pouvoir en RDC et analyse les conséquences de la faillite de la Samir sur la politique énergétique marocaine.

Alliés lointains, voisins hostiles : en Éthiopie, le pari diplomatique à haut risque d’Abiy Ahmed. Addis-Abeba cultive l’art des alliances transversales, séduisant simultanément l’Occident, la Chine et les pays du Golfe. Une agilité qui trouve ses limites face aux rivalités de la Corne de l’Afrique.

Après la rupture, Alger en dit plus sur les « ingérences » reprochées aux Émirats arabes unis. Pour justifier sa rupture diplomatique avec Abou Dhabi, Alger a notamment mis en avant des « ingérences » émiraties dans sa vie politique. Selon certaines sources, les soupçons portent sur des tentatives d’empêcher la victoire d’Abdelmadjid Tebboune aux présidentielles de 2019 et de 2024.

Secrétariat général de l’ONU : un troisième vote défavorable à Macky Sall. Au terme du troisième « straw poll » tenu au sein du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies vendredi 18 septembre, l’ex-président sénégalais accuse un net recul dans la course à la succession d’António Guterres.

Minerais critiques en RDC : des acteurs chinois toujours plus présents… et nombreux. Les entreprises de l’empire du Milieu sont désormais parties prenantes dans 49 projets miniers critiques en RDC. Un chiffre inédit.

Centrafrique : Hassan Bouba, l’ex-rebelle que Touadéra ne veut pas écarter. De Berbérati à Birao, l’ancien rebelle continue de s’afficher en homme de terrain. Passé à l’Urbanisme lors du dernier remaniement, le ministre reste un élément-clé des dossiers sécuritaires, en particulier depuis l’offensive sur Amdafok.

Comment Ceuta nourrit le discours de l’extrême droite européenne. La ruée vers Ceuta de dizaines de milliers de Marocains fin juillet a mis le feu aux poudres en Europe. Pour François Soudan, qui commente au micro de RFI l’article de notre collaboratrice Nina Kozlowski, ce « scénario idéal » profite avant tout aux droites identitaires occidentales.

Éthiopie-Égypte : les nouveaux barrages de la colère. Un an après son inauguration, le Grand barrage de la Renaissance (GERD) dépasse ses objectifs. Mais ses succès économiques attisent les tensions avec l’Égypte, qui menace de bloquer de nouveaux projets de l’Éthiopie sur le Nil.

Comment le Maroc devient le pivot de la stratégie militaire américaine en Afrique. Plus de pays signataires ou une coopération approfondie avec les membres existants, notamment le Maroc ? Évoquant la nouvelle phase des accords d’Abraham, l’Allison Center for National Security de la Heritage Foundation opte clairement pour la deuxième voie.

Wagner et Africa Corps en Centrafrique : qui compose l’assurance russe de Touadéra ?. Pionnier de l’alliance avec les bras armés du Kremlin en Afrique, Wagner puis Africa Corps, le président centrafricain a réuni autour de lui des spécialistes de la sécurité mais aussi des professionnels de la propagande ou des exportations minières. Revue de troupes.

Afrique du Sud : l’ANC va-t-elle perdre de vieux et stratégiques alliés ?. À l’approche des élections locales du 4 novembre, le Congrès national africain (ANC) pourrait perdre le soutien de deux organisations alliées depuis la lutte contre l’apartheid. Autre mauvaise nouvelle : l’érosion de son électorat s’accélère.

Un journaliste sud-africain et son fixeur portés disparus à Djibouti. Micah Reddy et son fixeur Kooki Mahmoud sont portés disparus depuis samedi 19 septembre. Alors que leurs soutiens appellent les autorités à « clarifier l’endroit où ils se trouvent », un responsable gouvernemental a déclaré ne pas être au courant de l’affaire.

Cameroun : face à l’aile dure du pouvoir, le dialogue politique est-il encore possible ?. Une semaine après la démission surprise de Maurice Kamto, une partie du Cameroun s’interroge sur l’avenir de son opposition. Derrière cet événement se dessine un tableau alarmant : celui d’un espace démocratique qui se rétrécit.

Législatives au Maroc : la réforme du Code de la famille, grand absent de la campagne. À quelques jours des législatives du 23 septembre, les féministes de Kif Mama Kif Baba ont passé au crible les programmes de huit partis sur trois sujets sensibles du Code de la famille. Leur constat : les engagements précis restent rares.

Air Sénégal : jusqu’où l’État pourra-t-il maintenir sa perfusion ?. Retards, avions saisis, ligne New York fermée : Air Sénégal accumule les déboires. Derrière le naufrage opérationnel se pose une question centrale : qui financera les neuf Boeing 737 MAX commandés pour relancer la compagnie ?

Municipales 2027 au Sénégal : Keur Massar va-t-il se retourner contre Diomaye Faye et Sonko ?. Pastef y a fait le plein de voix lors de la présidentielle et des législatives, en 2024. Deux ans plus tard, nombre d’élus et d’habitants de Keur Massar, département stratégique de l’est de la région de Dakar, semblent déchanter. Mais les jeux sont loin d’être faits.

Maroc-Algérie : deux diplomaties à l’offensive en Mauritanie. Routes, commerce, énergie, sécurité, Sahel… Rabat et Alger redoublent d’attention envers leur voisin mauritanien. À la manœuvre, Nasser Bourita et Ahmed Attaf incarnent deux diplomaties et deux projets régionaux concurrents. Face à eux, Nouakchott cultive méthodiquement l’art de ne pas choisir.

Comment la Banque européenne d’investissement repense sa stratégie africaine. Avec 3 milliards d’euros investis en Afrique en 2025, la Banque européenne d’investissement tient le cap dans un contexte de baisse structurelle de l’aide au développement. Elle joue désormais la carte géopolitique face à la Chine et aux fonds du Golfe.

Israël et le Maroc vont ouvrir des ambassades dans leurs pays respectifs, annonce la diplomatie de l’Etat hébreu. Le ministère israélien a aussi annoncé que des accords économiques seraient conclus entre les deux pays, qui disposent de bureaux de liaison, avant la fin de 2026, ainsi qu’une extension des vols directs entre le Maroc et Israël.

Dans le sud de l’Angola, le spectre d’une nouvelle sécheresse sous l’effet du « Super El Niño ». Depuis une dizaine d’années, l’Afrique australe est aux premières loges du dérèglement climatique. La situation pourrait encore s’aggraver avec le phénomène océanographique qui trouve son origine dans le Pacifique sud.

« Oui à l’excision » : la poussée réactionnaire qui secoue l’Afrique de l’Ouest. Portée par des campagnes virales et des relais d’opinion, la défense de l’excision gagne du terrain en Afrique de l’Ouest. Une résurgence des discours conservateurs qui fragilise des décennies de lutte contre les mutilations génitales féminines.

Du gouvernement à l’armée, le général Tiani resserre les rangs après la tentative de putsch au Niger. Depuis le 29 août, le chef de la junte a remplacé quatre ministres, démis de ses fonctions le chef d’état-major des armées et procédé à l’arrestation d’au moins 200 militaires.

En Guinée, la chaîne France 24 interdite de diffusion après qu’un présentateur a qualifié le chef de l’Etat, Mamadi Doumbouya, de « président putschiste ». Depuis l’arrivée au pouvoir du général Doumbouya, les principaux partis politiques ont été dissous, les manifestations, interdites, sont réprimées et de nombreux dissidents ont été arrêtés, condamnés, poussés à l’exil ou sont portés disparus.

Excision : la poussée réactionnaire qui secoue l’Afrique de l’Ouest. En 2023, une étude publiée dans la revue Nature, estimait que l’ablation partielle ou totale du clitoris, des petites ou des grandes lèvres ou encore l’infibulation – les différentes formes de l’excision –, causaient environ 44 000 décès par an dans quinze pays africains, dont le Mali.

De Sidiki Diabaté à Sona Jobarteh, un nouveau souffle pour la kora. L’instrument à cordes ouest-africain voit son public rajeunir et son répertoire évoluer, comme l’illustre le concert parisien du musicien malien, qui se produit vendredi 18 septembre à l’Accor Arena, la salle parisienne de 20 000 places.

Nigeria : enquête après la mort en détention de 37 hommes soupçonnés d’être des mineurs illégaux. Le gouverneur de l’Etat du Niger, dans le centre du pays, où affluent des milliers de chercheurs d’or artisanaux, a décrété trois jours de deuil et reporté le début de la campagne pour les élections prévues en janvier.

Des affrontements interethniques font 26 morts dans la région d’Abyei, que se disputent les deux Soudans. Des assassinats au sein de deux ethnies ont « exacerbé les tensions entre les deux communautés », a affirmé la mission de maintien de la paix de l’ONU pour ce territoire.

Au Maghreb, des fractures géopolitiques de plus en plus inquiétantes. La rivalité s’exacerbe entre le Maroc et l’Algérie, qui investissent massivement dans leur armement. Ce duel se prolonge au Sahel et ce alors que les tensions hispano-marocaines autour de Ceuta alourdissent davantage le climat régional.

L’expulsion « en urgence absolue » de l’influenceur algérien « Doualemn » annulée par le tribunal administratif de Paris. Le tribunal ne s’étant pas prononcé sur la demande d’annulation d’un second arrêté d’expulsion qui n’invoquait pas l’urgence absolue, l’influenceur algérien peut toujours être potentiellement renvoyé de France.

Dans le centre du Mali, les djihadistes du GSIM relancent des offensives d’envergure. Trois attaques importantes d’installations militaires, intervenues coup sur coup, confirment le danger que fait peser la franchise sahélienne d’Al-Qaida sur la junte de Bamako.

L’ouverture conjointe d’ambassades au Maroc et en Israël, une annonce historique contestée dans le royaume. Depuis le rétablissement de leurs relations officielles, en 2020, les deux pays ne disposent que de bureaux de liaison. Aucune précision n’a été donnée sur le calendrier d’ouverture de ces chancelleries.

Au Mali, au moins 100 militaires et cinq mercenaires russes tués dans une attaque djihadiste, selon un dernier bilan. L’attaque, revendiquée par le Groupe de soutien de l’islam et des musulmans (GSIM), affilié à Al-Qaida, a eu lieu le 10 septembre et a visé un camp militaire à Dioura, dans le centre du pays.

A Ceuta, les centres d’accueil pour migrants sont saturés dès leur ouverture par les autorités. Cinquante jours après l’afflux dans la ville espagnole de plus de 70 000 immigrés illégaux en provenance du Maroc, Madrid dit avoir créé plus de 6 000 places sous des tentes. Il resterait entre 3 000 et 8 000 personnes à la rue.

Les guerres d’Ousmane Dillo, opposant tchadien, « général » au Soudan et en quête de justice à Paris. L’ancien officier de l’armée tchadienne, qui a également la nationalité française, tient le président tchadien, Mahamat Idriss Déby, pour responsable de l’assassinat d’une partie de sa famille.

En Ethiopie, le gouvernement restreint le minage de bitcoins pour préserver les eaux du Nil. Les entreprises de création de la cryptomonnaie, chinoises pour l’essentiel, sont massivement installées dans ce pays de la Corne de l’Afrique, profitant de son fort potentiel hydroélectrique. Mais la sécheresse provoquée par le phénomène océanographique El Niño diminue les capacités des barrages.

« J’ai failli repartir de chez eux sans mon bébé » : l’aide des grands-parents, cruciale mais parfois oppressante pour les mères kényanes. « Darons d’ailleurs ». Deux fois par mois, un de nos journalistes à l’étranger explore la parentalité hors de nos frontières. Au Kenya, il est fréquent que les parents vivant en ville confient leur enfant aux bons soins des grands-parents installés à la campagne. Une solution aussi rassurante que douloureuse pour certaines mères.

Zeinab Badawi, essayiste : « Que les Africains prennent conscience de leur histoire peut participer à une renaissance du continent ». La documentariste et universitaire britanno-soudanaise Zeinab Badawi publie en France « Une histoire africaine de l’Afrique », qui s’extrait du prisme occidental de l’esclavage et de la colonisation et propose « un récit accessible et exhaustif englobant tout le continent », explique-t-elle dans un entretien au « Monde ».

Zeinab Badawi, essayiste : « Que les Africains prennent conscience de leur histoire peut participer à une renaissance du continent ». La documentariste et universitaire britanno-soudanaise Zeinab Badawi publie en France « Une histoire africaine de l’Afrique », qui s’extrait du prisme occidental de l’esclavage et de la colonisation et propose « un récit accessible et exhaustif englobant tout le continent », explique-t-elle dans un entretien au « Monde ».

Le « super El Niño » qui arrive pourrait effacer 20 milliards de dollars de croissance en Afrique. Le phénomène météorologique devrait provoquer fortes pluies et inondations à l’Est, sécheresse au Sud et renforcer les vents secs à l’Ouest. Les récoltes mais aussi les voies de transport, donc le commerce, seront affectées.

L’Afrique face à un « super El Niño » qui pourrait effacer 20 milliards de dollars de croissance. Le phénomène météorologique devrait provoquer fortes pluies et inondations à l’Est, sécheresse au Sud et renforcer les vents secs à l’Ouest. Les récoltes mais aussi les voies de transport, donc le commerce, seront affectées.

Allemagne : le parti de Friedrich Merz a essuyé une défaite historique aux élections régionales. Pour la première fois depuis 1949, l’Union chrétienne-démocrate (CDU), parti du chancelier, est passée sous les 5 % lors d’un scrutin régional, dans le Land de Mecklembourg-Poméranie-Occidentale, quorum requis pour être représentée au Parlement régional.

Au Maroc, les faux-semblants d’une campagne législative sans relief. Le scrutin législatif du 23 septembre ne suscite que peu d’intérêt dans le royaume, où le thème du coût de la vie est la préoccupation dominante parmi les électeurs. Les partis favoris, proches du palais royal, se contentent d’une campagne de façade.

War on Iran: How the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps underpins the republic Submitted by Daniel Tester on Thu, 09/17/2026 - 13:07 The IRGC has been core to Tehran's influence at home and abroad, not least through Quds Force Members of the IRGC stand in formation during a "Sacred Defence Week" parade in Tehran in September 2019 (AFP/Iranian presidency handout) On Often called a state within a state, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is a deeply conservative organisation that has underpinned Iran’ s establishment for decades and directed much of its response to attacks by the US and Israel this year. Conceived as a protector of the Iranian revolution, the guard has hundreds of thousands of troops who are distinct from Iran’s official army. It is also unelected, sitting alongside Iran’s elected officials under the ultimate authority of the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei . The IRGC was founded in March 1979 by commanders of the conservative militias that helped overthrow the western-backed Shah Reza Pahlavi the previous month. Known as the Pasdaran (“guardians”) or Sepah (“legion”) in Persian, it was established to protect the new political order and to counterbalance Iran’s army, which retained links to the deposed monarchy and, many feared, might stage a coup d’etat. The IRGC sidelined the leftist factions that helped overthrow the shah, which it opposed ideologically and saw as close to the USSR . Today, the guard has five main arms: a ground army, an air force, a navy, an elite overseas wing called Quds Force (meaning “Jerusalem force”) and a volunteer paramilitary called Basij (meaning “mobilisation”). It is estimated to have 150,000-plus active personnel, plus Basij volunteers who serve as part-time reserves, and whose numbers range from anywhere between 100,000 and 1m. For comparison, Iran’s official army, known domestically as Artesh, has around 600,000 troops. The IRGC also controls Iran’s ballistic missiles, which it has used to attack Israel, and is tasked with safeguarding border security and the country’s nuclear facilities. What is the IRGC’s domestic role? Besides its military role, the guard is embedded in all aspects of life in Iran, from business and politics to education and even sport . Many IRGC veterans hold senior roles in government and parliament, and can determine the success or failure of an individual's job application or business venture. Through Basij, the corps has plainclothes volunteers in neighbourhoods, schools and universities who serve to uphold conservative religious values. Critics have termed the force a “morality police”. Basij volunteers have also clamped down on political opposition figures and crushed public demonstrations, such as the 1999 student protests , the 2009 Green Movement , and the 2024-2025 protests , when thousands of civilians were killed. A protest in Tehran for Mahsa Amini, who died after being arrested, on 19 September 2022 (obtained by AFP) But the IRGC also provides social services ( such as after natural disasters ) and employment for hundreds of thousands in rural areas, gaining it supporters among parts of the population. As an economic force, the IRGC holds hundreds of government contracts, many of which were awarded under the conservative president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (2005-13). Through these, it has developed monopolies over industries and now receives an estimated 50 percent of revenues from Iran’s oil sector. Thomas Juneau , professor at the University of Ottawa’s Graduate School of Public and International Affairs, told Middle East Eye that the corps’ business interests “allow the IRGC and its sympathisers to themselves profit, to have access to pots of cash with which they can buy off the loyalty of others, and to marginalise competing business interests. “In that sense, the IRGC has both a vested interest in the survival of the Islamic Republic and its web of cronyism, as well as the means to protect its survival.” What does the IRGC do outside Iran? Through Quds Force, the IRGC has long helped fund and supply a network of regional groups that Tehran has dubbed its “ Axis of Resistance ”. These include Hamas in occupied Palestine , Hezbollah in Lebanon , parts of the Hashd al-Shaabi (Popular Mobilisation) umbrella group in Iraq , and Ansar Allah in Yemen , better known as the Houthis. Support for Palestine has long been core to the IRGC, and each of these groups has sought to counter Israeli, US and Saudi influence in the region. Hamas has fought several wars with Israel and launched the 7 October attacks in 2023; Hezbollah has battled Israel since the 1980s; and the Houthis have hit Israel with drone attacks and blocked shipping lanes in the Red Sea. Nonetheless, each group retains some independence from Tehran, which for instance denied involvement in Hamas’s 7 October attack - a claim US intelligence has supported . Members of Syria's military in Aleppo on 7 January 2020 mourning the US assassination of Iranian military commander Qasem Soleimani (AFP) The IRGC also supported Bashar al-Assad in Syria prior to and during the civil war , during which hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions more forced from their homes. Syria under Assad also long served as a supply channel for Iranian weapons for Hezbollah in Lebanon until his fall in December 2024. How did the IRGC become so powerful? One of the guard's first major roles after the 1979 revolution was suppressing armed rebellions by Kurdish and other minority ethnic groups. From 1980 until 1988, tens of thousands were killed during the Iran-Iraq War amid battles, minefields and chemical weapons. Sina Azodi , assistant professor of Middle East politics at George Washington University’s Elliott School of International Affairs, told Middle East Eye that the conflict was pivotal in the guard's development. “The current Iranian political leadership were the volunteers of the Iran-Iraq war who with very basic training went to the front lines with nothing more than assault rifles.” A damaged Iranian tank, decorated with a portrait of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, on the Iran-Iraq border in September 1980 (AFP) The IRGC's current worldview, he says, was shaped by its memory of the international support for Saddam Hussein's Iraq that it confronted during the conflict. "Their mindset is shaped by those traumas and the need for Iran to be able to stand on its own feet to defend the country." The IRGC was tasked with reconstruction after the war, seeing its role grow under new supreme leader Ali Khamenei and expanding an intelligence arm that now rivals the Ministry of Intelligence. Much of the IRGC’s international network was laid by Qassem Soleimani , Quds Force leader from 1998 until his assassination by the US in 2020 and regarded as the second most powerful person in Iran after Khamenei. His killing shocked the IRGC. Five days later, it shot down a Ukrainian commercial passenger plane as it left Tehran’s main airport, killing 176 people onboard. It later apologised , saying that it mistook the aircraft for a military plane. What action has been taken against the group? The IRGC is regarded as an adversary by many regional Arab-majority governments and much of the West, where it has long been sanctioned . Many governments have gone further, designating the IRGC as a terrorist group, which typically makes it a criminal offence to communicate with, trade with or express support for it or its affiliates. The US was the first to proscribe the Quds Force in 2007, and banned the IRGC altogether in 2019 during the first administration of President Donald Trump. Some officials in the Pentagon and the CIA privately opposed the Trump move: it is diplomatically unusual to ban official parts of other governments. The US considered delisting the IRGC during the Biden administration. But other countries soon followed suit. Canada proscribed the IRGC in 2024, as did the EU in January 2026 after the mass killing of Iranian protesters. The EU move, led by Italy and supported by France and Spain, has been followed by European countries outside the bloc. The UK proscribed the guard in July amid pressure from the US, years of lobbying from pro-Israel and Iranian diaspora groups, and attacks on Jewish groups in London that the UK government has linked to the IRGC. In total, 23 countries, aside from the 27 EU members, have designated the IRGC as a terrorist organisation, including Argentina, Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Israel, Saudi Arabia and Ukraine. While more than a hundred others have not sanctioned the IRGC, ties with the rest of the world are restricted by secondary sanctions imposed by the US, which sanction any firm that trades with any IRGC affiliates. The measures have led Iran and the IRGC to strengthen relations with US rivals that have similarly been cut off from the US-dominated financial system, or have enough economic heft to weather potential US retaliation. The IRGC has sold weapons to Russia throughout its invasion of Ukraine and jet fuel to Myanmar’s junta during the country’s civil war. Iran sells much of its crude oil to China via a so-called “shadow fleet” that aims to skirt US sanctions. Who are the IRGC's key figures? Many of the IRGC’s top personnel have been assassinated by the US and Israel in recent years. Key to its survival has been its succession strategy, with Juneau saying it "has long had extensive contingency plans to replace killed commanders". Its highest rank is commander-in-chief, one of several IRGC roles directly appointed by the supreme leader. Ahmad Vahidi , previously Iran’s minister of defence, has held that position since his predecessor, Mohammed Pakpour, was killed by Israel in March. He in turn succeeded Hossein Salami whom Israel killed in the June 2025 war. From left to right: IRGC leaders Ahmad Vahidi (2026), Esmail Qaani (2024) and Hossein Taeb (2018) (all AFP) Esmail Qaani has led Quds Force since Soleimani’s 2020 assassination. Hossein Taeb , a cleric and former intelligence chief, is current head of Basij after Israel killed Gholamreza Soleimani (no relation to Qassem) in March. Others killed by Israel include Alireza Tangsiri, commander of the IRGC Navy, on 26 March, and Majid Khademi, head of the IRGC’s intelligence wing, on 6 April. Israeli airstrikes have also targeted more moderate figures, including Ali Larijani, a pragmatic politician who headed Iran’s security council until he was assassinated by Israel on 17 March. It is now led by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr , a longtime IRGC hardliner. How has the IRGC been hurt by the war? Juneau says that “on the one hand, the IRGC has been badly hit by the US and Israel during the war, as have other pillars of the Islamic Republic”. “If we simply count strikes, military installations damaged or destroyed, ships or aircraft damaged or destroyed, then we can conclude that the IRGC has been significantly weakened,” he says. But the guard “has prepared for this war for decades”, he adds. “The US and Israel have destroyed an important proportion of the IRGC's missiles and drones, but the force still has more than enough to continue threatening shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.” For this reason, Juneau says the IRGC is far from admitting defeat, with many hardliners believing they have the upper hand and seeing no need to make compromises. “The way out of the war to the IRGC is to consolidate and institutionalise its geopolitical gains. “It wants, in particular, to see a new arrangement in the Persian Gulf whereby it can de facto veto maritime traffic.” War on Iran How the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps underpins Iran Explainers Post Date Override 0 Update Date Mon, 05/04/2020 - 21:29 Update Date Override 0

Qatar pushes for revival of US-Iran talks, warns against ‘cycles of escalation’ Qatar is working to restart negotiations between the United States and Iran, its foreign ministry said on Sunday, as the prime minister warned that regional security cannot rest on repeated confrontation. A ministry spokesperson said Qatari officials were “shuttling between capitals” in the hope of making progress, and that Doha had received assurances from US administration officials that Washington wants to reach an agreement. The spokesperson called for a regional solution that delivers stability, alongside an international understanding that protects waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking also on Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani said lasting security could not be built through "repeated cycles of escalation and retaliation", nor through "arrangements that leave any state vulnerable to the absence of security". He called for a framework in which sovereignty is respected, and no state can pose a "threat to another", adding that Qatar “had worked with regional and international partners to keep channels of communication open and reduce tensions.” In a statement, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry has condemned the storming of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound by Ben Gvir and Israeli settlers on Sunday, saying “repeated provocations will fuel cycles of violence and escalation in the region”.

The Houthi strikes exposed how vulnerable the Gulf kingdom is to the Yemeni group’s recent wave of attacks on the country, which they say are a response to Saudi strikes on Yemen. Will US President Donald Trump assist his friend Mohammed bin Salman? The crown prince - who the US president failed to help when oil terminals were hit by missiles from Iraq in 2019 - called the White House asking for US support in its war with Ansar Allah (Houthis). Once again, Trump said no. The $600bn that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman committed to investing in the US in his deals with Trump last year has bought almost zero protection from the world’s military superpower. The administration offered to share intelligence and assist Riyadh with targeting operations, but Trump desperately wants to avoid opening any new fronts, with US forces overstretched in the blockade of Iran . (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Instead, Trump made a deal with the group that had fought the Saudi coalition to a standstill in Yemen after a devastating eight-year war. Under the terms recently agreed in Muscat, Houthi leaders confirmed they would uphold a 2025 ceasefire with the US , ensuring the Red Sea remains open to global shipping, except for Saudi vessels. In sum, the Houthis would continue the war with Saudi Arabia, and the US would stay out of it. Mohammed bin Salman was politely thrown under the bus. Meanwhile, military commanders from the US and aligned Arab states were reportedly brought together with their Israeli counterparts in Germany - a secret meeting organised by US Central Command (Centcom) to discuss the Iran war . Israel then leaked the meeting. Sources told Israeli journalist Barak Ravid that the “private retreat” was organised by Centcom commander Admiral Brad Cooper, and attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE , Bahrain , Kuwait , Qatar , Jordan and Egypt . Unreliable partners Any time Arab states secretly meet with Israeli officials, they should by now realise that it will not remain so, due to Israel’s predilection for boasting. Israel doesn’t do discreet diplomacy. It’s no secret that pro-western Arab states have been doing under-the-counter deals with “the Zionist entity” for decades. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Earlier this month, Houthi fighters launched a rapid assault from southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, capturing the Red Sea port of Mocha overnight. They then advanced to capture the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Perim Island - a strategic point overseeing the vital waterway - as Saudi-backed government troops withdrew. Washington is not yet ready to treat its opponents as sovereign states with legitimate interests, and to cut lasting deals with them The fighting was bloody. Anti-Houthi National Resistance Forces reported that more than 500 of their fighters were killed and 1,500 injured . Clashes continue near Mocha and other fronts. Saudi strikes on Yemen’s Houthi forces have been met with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The key East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea has been hit. But Riyadh’s new Mecca defence pact allies, Turkey and Pakistan , have not come to its aid. If not them and not Washington, then who? Enter Benjamin Netanyahu, who has offered military and intelligence assistance to the Gulf states. Saudi Arabia is already getting intelligence from Israel via the US on the Yemenis, according to Kan. Still, Riyadh does not see Israel as a reliable military partner, says Gulf analyst Andreas Krieg. “Riyadh does not want to move from dependence on Washington to dependence on an Israeli security architecture,” he told The New Arab . Fears that Iran's Yemeni allies will close off the main route for energy and shipping through the Red Sea, on top of the semi-paralysed Strait of Hormuz, have caused further spikes in oil and diesel prices . A senior Israeli intelligence source told Al-Monitor : “At the moment, no one has deterrence over the Houthis. Not the Americans, not us, and certainly not the Saudis. They are the dark horse that no one expected.” Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has agreed to send military advisers to Saudi Arabia, raising fears that the UK could once again be drawn into a Saudi war on Yemen . Trump will not intervene for Mohammed bin Salman, but he will sell billions of dollars worth of F-35s and one-tonne bombs to Riyadh . The US has just signed off on massive shipments of bombs to both Israel and Saudi Arabia. For Saudi Arabia, the Trump administration approved a $5bn package including 10,000 JDAM guidance kits and 10,000 bombs, split evenly between 500lb munitions and 2,000lb BLU-117s. For Israel, the $2.8bn US taxpayer-funded shipment includes 40,000 bombs - half BLU-117s and half MK-84s - and 20,000 penetrator warheads for hardened targets. It is the largest single transfer of this type of bomb to Israel in years. The scale of these planned shipments is terrifying, as American commentator Tucker Carlson recently pointed out , dwarfing the equivalent tonnage of the Second World War US bombings of Tokyo and Hiroshima. Like those airborne atrocities, the bombs will likely be used against defenceless civilians in Gaza , Lebanon and Yemen. How to end the war How can this latest escalation be brought to an end? Ansar Allah, which governs more than 70 percent of Yemen’s population, insists that the war can be stopped by lifting the 12-year-old Saudi blockade on Yemen . Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior Houthi spokesperson, told Sky News that Sanaa was seeking “to end the blockade and to end the aggression against Yemenis … The ball is in the Saudis’ court; it is their decision to stop this war.” He added: “All we have done is put the equation of a blockade for a blockade”, referring to the Saudi air, land and sea cordon around Yemen, which has starved its people and caused untold suffering, leading to tens of thousands of deaths . Saudi-Yemen conflict: The notion of an 'American saviour' is dead Read More » In the words of US journalist Ryan Grim , the solution to the wider conflict is simple, if unpalatable for Washington: “End the wars and treat Yemen and Iran like sovereign nations with an equal place in the world. (And also stop Israel’s attacks on southern Lebanon.) That’s it. That’s basically all they’d have to do. Just stop insisting on domination.” Put this way, it is extraordinary how the US can disguise its actions, and those of its allies, as defensive, when in fact it has been waging a decades-long war on Iran using sanctions, assassinations, sabotage and blockades. This conflict is now longer than the Cold War. The US empire has yet to reach a point of realism, where it can retreat from its unbridled supremacy with grace. And yet, six weeks out from the midterm elections, Trump needs to find a way to wind down the Middle East war he helped start with Netanyahu, and to tamp down record fuel prices for Americans - hence the deal with the Houthis. Washington is not yet ready to treat its opponents as sovereign states with legitimate interests, and to cut lasting deals with them. The June memorandum with Iran looked promising, but almost immediately, Trump ripped it up. Yet after November’s midterm elections, when Republicans are likely to be punished for Trump’s war, that may begin to change. Trillion-dollar defence bills are piling up the national debt, while global holders of US treasuries are offloading them at a worrying rate. After the 2028 presidential election, perhaps Trump or his successor will do as former President Richard Nixon did, and make peace with Washington’s enemies. But they would have to cut Israel loose to do it. The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye. A Pew Research Center survey conducted weeks into the war on Iran found that six in 10 Americans now hold an unfavourable view of Israel, up from 53 percent last year and 42 percent in 2022. Gaza death toll climbs to 73,914 as four more Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks At least four Palestinians were killed and 17 wounded in Israeli attacks across the Gaza Strip over the past 24 hours, Gaza’s health ministry said on Monday. The ministry said one of those killed died of earlier wounds, while three bodies were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings. The latest figures bring the reported Palestinian death toll since 7 October 2023 to 73,914, while over 174,952 others have been reported wounded. Since the ceasefire took effect in October, the ministry has recorded 1,394 deaths, as 834 bodies have been recovered from the rubble. Thousands of victims remain under the debris and on roads because of the Israeli blockade on heavy machinery required by rescue teams, which have been unable to reach them. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs has reported that Israeli air strikes and other attacks have continued to cause casualties and damage in populated areas, while shortages of critical medical supplies and restrictions on humanitarian access continue to put pressure on Gaza’s health system.
