Strategic stability. IN a world awash with violence, where the old geopolitical rules of the game are being rapidly rewritten, there is a need for states to display maturity and rational behaviour in statecraft. This is all the more true in troubled regions such as South Asia, which have been witnessing friction for decades, and where nuclear weapons are part of the equation. Addressing a workshop in Islamabad recently, adviser to the National Command Authority and former head of the Strategic Plans Division retired Lt-Gen Mazhar Jamil highlighted the shrinking space for diplomacy in South Asia. He added that the erosion of arms control frameworks and reliance on hard power were creating “new challenges to strategic stability in South Asia”. While criticising India’s “military adventurism and hegemonic approaches”, the official made a crucial observation: there was no space for war between two nuclear states. This should be clear to any level-headed individual. However, high-level officials in the Indian military, as well as the political elite, have — particularly since last year’s hostilities — been making increasingly jingoistic statements directed at Pakistan. In May, the Indian army chief — who has since retired — hurled unacceptable threats at this country, which were described by ISPR as “hubristic”. Indian political leaders have been making similarly unhinged comments. While such language may attract a few votes and please extremist lobbies within India, it does lasting damage to the cause of peace in South Asia, especially at a time when both nations have only recently emerged from a dangerous encounter that could have spiralled into all-out war. War in a nuclear neighbourhood is not an option. Pakistani officials have reiterated this, and there is a need for similar rational behaviour from responsible military and civilian actors in India. There is huge bilateral mistrust at the moment. Yet to prevent a catastrophe in the subcontinent, both sides, particularly India, need to restart the dialogue process. This can begin with small steps, such as regular contact between military officials from both sides to ensure misunderstandings do not escalate into something larger. In parallel, diplomatic contacts and Track II efforts need to be resumed. While it is difficult to foresee peace in the immediate future, such steps can at least help in conflict management, while ensuring that the channels of communication are kept open. But perhaps the biggest need is for Indian officials to stop their inflammatory rhetoric against Pakistan, which is even more irresponsible at a time when the flames of war are burning not too far from South Asia. Hopefully, restraint and sustained dialogue can lead to bilateral trust and peace between Pakistan and India. Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026

Dangers of a wider war. A DANGEROUS new front has opened in the Middle East war. Yemen and the Red Sea are now the latest battleground. This has widened the regional conflict and added another layer to the escalating confrontation between the US and Iran. The entry of new actors, Iran-aligned Ansarullah Houthis and Iraqi militias, poses a serious security and economic threat to Saudi Arabia. Oil prices have soared as a result and fuel supplies to global markets have become more uncertain. Diplomacy is deadlocked. Efforts to revive talks between the US and Iran had stalled before these developments. Now they appear to have hit a wall. The dramatic turn of events came with the Houthis’ lightning military offensive along Yemen’s west coast, which culminated in their capture of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait. This gave them control of a key shipping route. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces failed to prevent the advance and the loss of more strategic territory to the Houthis. At the same time, the Houthis launched attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. The vital East-West pipeline across Saudi Arabia was forced to close after a drone strike by Iraq-based militias. Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi control of another maritime chokepoint — the narrow Bab al-Mandeb strait — has severely constrained KSA’s ability to export oil. Tehran claims the Houthis are acting independently. Nevertheless, the action by the Houthis and Iraqi militias could have been coordinated by Iran to mount pressure on the US and counter its attempt to loosen Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz by American warships escorting more vessels through the waterway. It may also be a res­ponse to US economic warfare which is placing fur­ther strain on the Iranian economy. Multiple Saudi air strikes on the Houthis have failed to dislodge them from the territory they have seized across Yemen. The militia continues to control the entire western coast of the country along the Red Sea. The fighting marks the re-eruption of a conflict that began in 2014 in Yemen’s civil war between a Saudi-led coalition spearheaded by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the Houthis. This came to a halt with a ceasefire in 2022. But the truce broke down this July when the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports following an attack on Sanaa airport by Saudi-backed forces. Beyond the economic fallout the political implications of a spreading conflict are also serious. The deteriorating situation confronts MBS with a dilemma: to escalate or pursue a diplomatic path. His efforts to secure US military intervention have not succeeded so far although there are unconfirmed reports that the US is weighing options to launch military strikes against the Houthis. He spoke twice to President Donald Trump asking for direct US help but Washington has been reluctant to join the fight. Trump’s comments during a visit to Ireland are revealing. “The Houthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said. “They don’t want us to go after them and would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through. It’s just one country they’re not too happy with. And we’ll get that straightened out.” The remarks indicate Trump’s unwillingness to intervene even as his most important Gulf ally comes under fierce attack. Washington clearly doesn’t want to shift focus from the conflict with Iran, where it is bogged down, having failed to gain the upper hand and compel Iran to submit to its demands. The US military is already overstretched and facing a serious munition shortfall after nearly seven months of war. These problems will worsen if the US intervenes in the Saudi-Houthis conflict. The US Central Comm­and estimates the Iran war has cost over $43 billion. Meanwhile, speculation that Riyadh may invoke the Makkah joint defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkiye has so far come to nothing. Pakistan has given no indication of going beyond verbal support to the kingdom and condemnation of Houthi actions even though it has troops and fighter jets deployed there. As the Foreign Office spokesman put it , the pact is defensive in nature and no military plan is under discussion. Prince Mohammed has however held talks with the Centcom chief amid reports that the US is helping KSA with targeting and intelligence. For all the assessments by many Western analysts that Iran’s regional allies have been weakened by the war with the US, the latest events show this is not the case. The ‘axis of resistance’ is not only intact but potent enough to launch a two-pronged assault on KSA plunging it into a crisis. Meanwhile, Iran’s leverage has increased because in addition to its grip over the Strait of Hormuz its ally, the Houthi militia, now controls the Red Sea energy chokepoint, Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which can be seen as a strategic gain for Tehran. The economic impact of an escalating wider conflict can be far-reaching. Already the oil price has soared to above $100 a barrel. Gas prices too have risen. Uncertainty about global energy supplies, which are already running low, may drive prices even higher. This despite the Houthi leadership’s assurance that it will not block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked ships. With its oil production having fallen, the world’s largest oil exporter, Saudi Arabia, has already cut crude oil shipments. The damage to its 1,200-kilometre export pipeline threatens the loss of four per cent of global oil supply. In the US, the oil price rise has contributed to pushing US borrowing costs to their highest level since 2007. The bond market is being adversely affected by fears over energy prices and inflation. Beyond the economic fallout for countries across the world, the political implications of a spreading conflict are no less serious. With new actors having entered the fray — and more might be sucked in — diplomacy will face new challenges in forging agreements among so many players. This will make the diplomatic process more complex and difficult even if there is willingness among the warring parties to find a negotiated end to the conflict. Unfortunately, a regional meeting in Oman between Iran and Gulf states to discuss control of the Strait of Hormuz and work out an interim arrangement has been postponed. For now, neither the US nor Iran are prepared to budge from their position and resume negotiations. In the end, the outcome may hinge on who can endure economic pain the longest. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026

Doctor, wife and three daughters found dead in Karachi apartment. • Foul smell emanating from family’s flat prompted neighbours to inform police • Doctors reserve opinion on cause of death until post-mortem examination is complete KARACHI: In a disturbing incident, a middle-aged doctor, his wife and their three underage daughters were found dead at their Ahsanabad apartment in Scheme-33 off Superhighway on Sunday, officials said. They added that the five partially decomposed bodies were recovered from the seventh floor of the high-rise building. The bodies were taken to the Abbasi Shaheed Hospital for a post-mortem examination. They were identified as 45-year-old Dr Umer and his 35-year-old wife, Mehwish. However, the police named only one daughter, 13-year-old Zainab, and said that two other girls were between the ages of two and four. Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed told Dawn there were no apparent injury marks on the bodies. She said the bodies were in advanced stage of decomposition. The cause of death was reserved for the chemical analysis. Dr Syed added that the doctors have collected samples for the DNA analysis. SITE Superhighway Industrial Area police SHO Mohammed Nawaz told Dawn that they received information from the union of the building that a foul smell was emanating from an apartment. The police rushed to the spot and saw the door locked from the inside. They broke open the door and found the five bodies lying in a room. The officer said that the doctor worked at a private hospital near his residence. He was recently diagnosed with cancer, which had reportedly upset him. He said recently robbers had also looted the doctor. The police officer said the family had been living there since 2024. East SSP Zubair Nazir Shaikh, who visited the spot, told Dawn that the bodies had been there for around three days. He said it would be premature to say anything about the exact cause of the death at this stage. He added that they were waiting for the post-mortem reports. Besides, he said, the crime scene unit was also called in to collect evidence while CCTV footage was also being obtained. He said investigators would take statements from the hospital management, where the doctor had worked, and neighbours to get clues about the circumstances surrounding the deaths. He said the doctor originally hailed from Punjab. The investigators have managed to contact his brother, who lives in Lahore. The police have also asked the doctor’s father-in-law, who also lives in Punjab, to claim the bodies. The SSP said the neighbours had told the police about the doctor’s medical condition and his difficult financial situation. However, further investigations are underway to verify the information, he added. Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026

Final frontiers. IN his first term in office, US President Donald Trump announced the creation of the Space Force, a new branch of the US military to add to the existing army, navy, air force, etc. Now, in 2026, not only has the US announced for the first time that it has actually put weapons in space, it has also released the uniforms designed for the Space Force. To no one’s surprise, they look identical to the uniforms of the Imperial Navy in Star Wars. In case you’ve been exiled to Alpha Centauri for the last century, those were the Bad Guys. Unfortunate Sith parallels aside, the US has not revealed the exact nature of the weaponry but US military leaders have previously spoken about the need for space-based military capabilities, purportedly to counter alleged Russian and Chinese capabilities. In particular, the US has been looking at anti-satellite systems designed to disable or blind an adversary’s eye-in-the-sky capabilities. That capability has been quite irksome for the US during its disastrous war on Iran, with reports claiming that Chinese and Russian satellites provided information for Iranian drone and missile strikes, enabling pinpoint accuracy when it comes to targeting US assets in the region. And then, a few weeks ago, an orbiting Chinese satellite — Yaogan-50 — disintegrated into over 40 pieces. Was this a coincidence or a demonstration of America’s now-declared capabilities? We’ll likely never know. Development of space-based weapons continues. What we do know is that China — which has protested against the US announcement — has tried to develop anti-satellite capabilities of its own likely based on the philosophy that while space-based weapons are difficult to deploy and expensive, countermeasures against enemy satellites may be an easier way out, similar to the philosophy of area denial by fielding anti-ship and aircraft carrier missiles. In 2007, China successfully targeted an aging weather satellite with a ground-based missile. Next year, the US followed suit by shooting down a military satellite it claimed was about to crash, and in 2010, China shot down another satellite. But since destroying satellites entirely can be messy, capabilities are being developed to ‘blind’ them instead, rendering them useless; along with the US, Russia and China are also developing and deploying ground-based directed-energy weapons and satellite-blinding lasers. The US is already deploying the Meadowlands Counter Communication System which can fry orbital satellites using electromagnetic beams. In one sense, the first shot in the Space Wars was fired in World War II when German scientists created the V1 and V2 rocket and missile, the predecessors of the cruise and ballistic missiles, but the real push to weaponise space began with the space race where the USSR scored early wins with the launch of Sputnik in 1957 and by making cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin the first man in space four years later. In 1962, the US conducted a high-altitude nuclear weapons test codenamed Starfish Prime — not just as a warning to the USSR but also to see if the resulting electromagnetic pulse would disrupt nearby satellites. With the spectre of nuclear weapons in space looming large and talk of potential military bases on the moon, the Outer Space Treaty was signed in 1967, prohibiting the placement of nuclear weapons or other WMDs and proclaiming that no country would seek sovereignty over the moon. But the development of space-based weapons continued nevertheless. In 1974, the Soviets successfully tested the first known armed satellite. The Salyut-3 satellite was equ­ip­ped with an air­craft cannon from which it fi­­­red a single rou­nd proving that it was ind­eed possible to arm satellites alth­o­ugh quest­ions of accura­cy and feasibility rem­­­­­ained. Over a decade later, the USSR returned to the concept by testing a heavy satellite — the Polyus — which was armed with a carbon-dioxide laser and a cannon to boot. However, it failed to launch. Then there was Reagan and his ‘Star Wars’ initiative that envisioned a national ballistic missile shield for the US, some components of which would be space-based: the ‘Brilliant Pebbles’ project envisioned the deployment of thousands of small interceptors in orbit that would then collide with Soviet ICBMs — a sort of Patriot Missile system in space. Other proposals included satellites armed with lasers. Whether or not Reagan knew, most of these plans were impossible to implement because of cost and lack of requisite technology. But the USSR took it seriously enough to try and play catch-up. Arguably, the costs thus incurred played a part in the downfall of the Soviet Empire. But this isn’t the Cold War anymore, and the rapid technological developments we are seeing now mean that ideas once safely relegated to the realm of science fiction are becoming fact. Watch the skies. The writer is a journalist. X: @zarrarkhuhro Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026

PPP wants CM Maryam to show aircraft rent details. LAHORE: Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) Lahore President Faisal Mir has demanded that the government disclose the details of the official account into which the alleged rent for the chief minister’s aircraft was deposited. He said Maryam Nawaz should show the nation the name of the bank, the account title, the account number and the receipt for the amount deposited. Speaking at the birthday ceremony of PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, here on Sunday, he said that if verifiable official records of the aircraft rental payment were not presented, it would be assumed that facts had been concealed from the nation. He said the PPP would approach the appropriate legal forum to establish the truth behind Maryam Nawaz’s statement and the alleged payment. He added that if the chief minister had misled the nation, action should also be taken against her in accordance with the constitution and the law. Stressing that the law is equal for everyone, he said the same principle under which Prime Minister Yusuf Raza Gilani was disqualified should also apply to the PML-N leader. He criticised the ruling party for allegedly giving concessions to the rich and inflation to the poor in every budget. He proposed an additional tax of at least Rs50,000 on vehicles above 1500cc so that the tax burden would fall on the wealthy rather than on the poor. Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026

Pakistan's table tennis teams face humbling opening to Asian Games. Pakistan’s table tennis teams endured a chastening opening two days at the Asian Games, with the women’s side crashing out of the group stage without winning a single match and the men’s team also losing both of their opening ties. The women’s team suffered a 3-0 defeat to India in their final Group F match at the Sky Hall Toyota on Monday, completing a miserable campaign that began with identical losses to Singapore and Indonesia on Sunday. Against India, 15-year-old Aleena Khan was dispatched in just 10 minutes, losing 11-3, 11-3, 11-4 to the experienced Sutirtha Mukherjee. Kulsoom Khan, 19, then fell in straight games, 11-6, 11-7, 11-5, to Syndrela Das, before Fatima Khan suffered the same fate against Sreeja Akula, India’s highest-ranked player, going down 11-4, 11-4, 11-5 in 11 minutes. Sunday’s defeats followed a similar pattern. Against Singapore, Aleena, Kulsoom and 55-year-old Nosheen Aslam all lost in straight games. Fatima, Kulsoom and Nosheen were then beaten in equally brutal fashion by Indonesia, leaving Pakistan without a single game won across the entire event. The men’s team fared little better. Pakistan lost both of their Sunday ties 3-0, against Iran and Indonesia, and face India later on Monday. Taha Bilal and Abbas Khan were unable to win a game in either match, though Mohammad Khan managed to take one game against Indonesia’s Mohammad Negara.

Putin's party set to retain power after Russia vote hit by cyberattacks, drones. Vladimir Putin’s ruling United Russia party won a large majority in the country’s parliamentary elections, marked by cyberattacks and a barrage of Ukrainian drone strikes, according to results published by state media early Monday. The election, held to elect members in all seats of the lower house State Duma, is the first since Moscow launched its large-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. No party opposed to the war was allowed to run, with Russia’s Supreme Court removing the anti-war Yabloko party off the ballot weeks before the vote. Voting also took place in Ukrainian territories occupied and annexed by Russia. Turnout could offer a barometer of public opinion towards Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II. According to results reported by Russian news agencies after just over 71 per cent of ballots were counted, United Russia took 57.5pc of the vote. The Communist Party and LDPR nationalists trailed behind on 14 and 8.7pc respectively. The ruling party is on course to retain its two-thirds majority of the 450 seats in the State Duma, allowing it to amend the constitution, according to projections by the state agency TASS. The first official results and turnout will be expected on Monday morning. Ukraine fired waves of drones at Moscow and the surrounding region on the final day of voting on Sunday, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze, officials said. Russia vowed it would “intensify” its strikes on Kyiv in response, with the defence ministry accusing Ukraine of attempting to “disrupt the democratic will of Russian citizens”. An exit poll published by a state-run pollster showed United Russia on course to win 49.4pc of the vote, close to the same amount it achieved in the previous election. “In response to the Kyiv regime’s attacks on civilian targets within Russia, the Russian army will continue and intensify its high accuracy strikes against military targets in Kyiv,” the Russian defence ministry said. Wave of Ukrainian drones The Ukrainian attack was the largest on Moscow since the start of the war and involved around 1,600 drones, 450 of which were aimed directly at the capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Images showed a gaping hole in a multi-storey apartment building on the outskirts of the capital, while another showed black smoke billowing from what appeared to be an oil refinery. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky praised the attacks, saying “our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night”. While diplomatic efforts to end the war have not prevented mutual strikes from escalating in recent months, Zelensky spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump, who in recent days has urged Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries. The pair are expected to meet in New York in the coming days. At least two people were killed — a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man — in two separate locations, Moscow regional Governor Andrey Vorobyov said. A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, Vorobyov added. Ukraine has targeted Russian infrastructure with drones throughout the war, in retaliation for Russian bombardment of its own towns and cities. Yabloko — a liberal party that had called for an end to the fighting — was barred from running its federal list by Russia’s Supreme Court, although its candidates remained on the ballot in some single-mandate constituencies. Putin had urged Russians to take part, casting the vote as a show of support for Moscow’s troops and an “answer to those who want to weaken Russia”. The Kremlin’s chief political opponents have been driven into exile, while Putin’s main rival, Alexei Navalny, died in an Arctic prison in 2024. Navalny’s widow Yulia Navalnaya called on anti-war Russians to collectively cast their ballots at noon on Sunday, a tactic that drew crowds in the 2024 presidential election. In Berlin and London, AFP reporters saw dozens of opposition supporters gathered outside Russian embassy buildings in protest at the vote. Cyberattacks As voting entered a final day, Russia’s electoral chief said there had been a wave of cyberattacks targeting election infrastructure. Ella Pamfilova, chair of Russia’s Central Election Commission, did not say who was responsible. The attacks appeared to have been carried out by “highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools,” she said. “Over the past period, more than 1,000 waves of DDoS attacks have been recorded against infrastructure in Russia that is specifically involved in the electoral process,” Pamfilova was quoted as saying by Russian news agencies. DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attacks involve overwhelming a system with internet traffic so that it is unable to function normally. She warned on Saturday that saboteurs had also severed communication lines in Russia’s far east, in an apparent attempt to frustrate the voting.

After Aleema, Imran’s sisters Uzma and Noreen also detained in Lahore under MPO for 30 days. Former prime minister and PTI founder Imran Khan’s sisters, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were detained for 30 days on Monday, ahead of the party’s September 27 protest call. The development follows the detention of Imran’s other sister, Aleema Khan, after Lahore’s deputy commissioner (DC) ordered her detention or arrest for 30 days on Sunday. The detention has come amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its September 27 countrywide protest and march to Islamabad, which the party has called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. In an order dated Sept 20, a copy of which is available with Dawn , the Lahore DC Office ordered that Noreen and Uzma be detained for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960, stating that the two were “prejudicial to the public safety and maintenance of public order”. The MPO ordinance allows the authorities to order detention and restrict judicial review of such orders. The two will remain in custody under the superintendent, Central Jail, Kot Lakhpat, it said. The order stated that the two were involved in the May 9 protest and “motivated the workers to damage public and government property”. “Moreover, they are again mobilising the workers through social media and public meetings to create a law and order situation, raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the government/institution in order to provoke and incite them,” the order read. “Accordingly, multiple cases including 96/23 PS Race Course were registered,” it said, stating that Uzma and Noreen were “potential dangers to public peace and tranquillity”. “Such activists will give rise to a situation prejudicial to public safety and maintenance of public order, if left unchecked.” The decision was taken in a meeting held on Sunday, under the chairmanship of the Lahore DC Muhammad Ali Ijaz, where the issue was discussed and members “endorsed” the “evidence” presented by the police. The order stated that the Lahore DC was convinced that Uzma and Noreen’s presence “at any public place will pose a grave threat to the public safety and will likely cause breach of public peace and public order”. In a post on X in the early hours of Monday, the party’s Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram had accused Punjab police of “arresting both sisters of Imran, along with their children and the sons of Aleema Khan”. Akram claimed that the individuals had “been placed in an armoured vehicle and are being taken to an unknown location”. PTI lawyer Awais Younas Chaudhry had confirmed to Dawn that all three of Imran’s sisters had been arrested. “Earlier Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan were confined to their house, but on Monday morning they were taken to an unknown place,” he claimed. PTI, in a post on X, condemned the alleged arrest, calling it a “blatant abuse of authority, a violation of fundamental rights, and an act of political victimisation”. “Such conduct is illegal, unconstitutional, and is condemned in the strongest possible terms,” the party said. Meanwhile, Imran’s son Kasim Khan, in a post on X, alleged that Uzma and Noreen had been “abducted”. “This is a disgrace,” Kasim wrote, claiming that authorities had “broken into my aunties and cousins houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation”. “No reasons for arrest have been stated. No news has been released as to where they have been taken,” he wrote. Speaking to Dawn , former member of the Punjab Assembly Seemabia Tahir said, “It was unfortunate that the family members [..] were facing such brutality”. She expressed hope that following this, “people will surely come out of their houses on Sept 27”. Aleema’s detention On Sunday, Aleema was detained under similar orders. The September 20 order, a copy of which is available with Dawn , said DC Ijaz had ordered the detention or arrest of Aleema and a man named Muhammad Ameer under the Punjab MPO. The MPO ordinance allows the authorities to order detention and restrict judicial review of such orders. Following the arrest, Aleema’s sister Noreen addressed a press conference in Lahore, flanked by her sister’s counsel, Advocate Mudassir Umar. Noreen claimed Aleema was “picked up” along with her driver after she left her residence on Saturday, and they later learnt that Aleema’s vehicle was parked at a police station. Meanwhile, the lawyer said they had yet to receive official confirmation of her arrest. Police sources had confirmed to Dawn on Sunday that Aleema was taken to Lahore’s Kot Lakhpat jail. Detentions ahead of Sept 27 protest The detentions come after a string of reported actions against the PTI in Punjab ahead of its September 27 protest. On Sunday, Sahiwal police arrested Asad Khan Baloch, former mayor of the municipal corporation and ex-ticket holder for PTI, along with the party’s city president in Sahiwal, Muhammad Shahid Chohan. PTI also claimed that MNAs Sanaullah Mastikhel , Ahsan Jamal Khan and Mian Ghous were taken into custody, according to the party’s information secretary. District authorities had also issued preventive detention orders against dozens of PTI workers under MPO a week ago, including 31 in one Punjab notification and a further 14 in Toba Tek Singh. Similar reports have come from Islamabad, where the PTI plans to march on the protest day. However, the government has vowed to stop the march, and the Islamabad High Court (IHC) has ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”.

Two officers among 6 martyred, 8 terrorists killed in Hangu fire exchange: ISPR. Two officers and four others were martyred while eight terrorists were killed in a fire exchange in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Hangu district on Sunday, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said. During an intense fire exchange between a “security forces convoy and Khwarij ”, 23-year-old Captain Abuzar Farooq from Gujranwala and 22-year-old Lieutenant Sheraz Babar of Chakwal, “who were leading their troops from the front, fought gallantly and paid the ultimate sacrifice and embraced martyrdom along with their four men”. According to images released by ISPR, the other four men comprised three sepoys and a “non-combatant”. On the other hand, “eight Khwarij belonging to Indian-sponsored Fitna al Khwarij were sent to hell due to effective engagement by own troops”, the ISPR statement added. The state uses the term Fitna al Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). A sanitisation operation was being conducted to eliminate any other terrorist found in the area, ISPR said. It affirmed that the “relentless counterterrorism campaign under vision ‘Azm-i- Istehkam’ (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”. “These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation at all costs,” the military’s media wing stated. Later in the evening, the funeral prayers of the martyred personnel were offered, following which, their bodies were dispatched to their native towns. Sunday’s development comes two days after a two-pronged assault near a mosque in the old Police Lines of KP’s Kohat district claimed 23 lives, including those of 17 policemen. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. KP witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks in August compared with July, according to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). On August 7, a captain was martyred while seven terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Hangu. On July 30, a deputy superintendent of police (DSP) was among nine cops martyred and 28 others were injured after terrorists attacked the Khazina Banda checkpost in Hangu. Days later, security forces were reported to have killed the mastermind behind the attack.

'I live in fear': 1.5 million Pakistani children sexually exploited online. Pakistani teenager Zara Shah was targeted by a stranger while playing a computer game, drawn into a conversation that would expose her to terrifying online sexual exploitation. Zara, whose name has been changed by AFP for safety reasons, is one of an estimated 1.5 million children in Pakistan who experienced online sexual abuse in one year, according to a report published by the UN children’s agency this month. “We started chatting while playing an online game, and he began acting like a friend. Later, he wanted to meet and, after, started asking me for nudes,” 17-year-old Shah said. “When I refused, he threatened to find my family online and tell them that we had been talking,” she added. According to the Unicef report, around 85 per cent of perpetrators were known to the victims, aged between 12 and 17. “The abuse may start with a friendly conversation, a gaming interaction, a promise of gifts, money or romance,” Daniel Kardefelt, lead author of the global Unicef report, told AFP . “Perpetrators may spend months building trust using information that they find on social media,” Kardefelt said. In Muslim-majority Pakistan, 71pc of victims did not tell anyone, according to the Unicef report, while no child surveyed reported the abuse through formal channels — including police, helplines or social workers. Their silence was mostly because of stigma, shame and fears over how their families or society may react. “Around 44pc of reported abuse was entirely online, with Snapchat and WhatsApp among the most common settings,” said Mehek Naeem, director of Pahchaan, a children’s rights organisation based in Lahore. Girls can face heightened risks of sexual extortion, which can lead to restrictions on their mobility or withdrawal from school. For Zara, the threat of being exposed to her family was enough to keep her silent. “I could have been stopped from going to school or leaving the house altogether,” she said. “Staying quiet felt like the better option than speaking up. But anxiety kills me every day.” Loopholes, ‘no implementation’ With around 74pc of children aged 12 to 17 in Pakistan estimated by Unicef to be internet users, concerns over online safety are growing as their access to digital platforms expands. Echoing other policies around the world, the provincial government in Punjab this month passed a resolution to bar children under 16 from using social media. However, it has faced opposition. “I disagree with the ban,” said Usama Khilji, a digital rights activist. “It will be a challenge to implement, and children can circumvent the ban through VPNs. Children have the right of freedom of expression, and a ban takes that away,” he said. Pakistan has a legal framework addressing tech-facilitated offences against children, but “there is no implementation”, said Tahira Afrasiyab, a spokesperson for non-profit organisation Muslim Hands. And, according to experts, there are loopholes in existing laws. Human rights lawyer Salman Afridi said this issue shows how “economic vulnerability can be weaponised” for amounts as small as Rs10,000 in exchange for the production of sexual content. “What we are seeing is the use of technology to facilitate an entire chain of grooming, inducement, coercion, blackmail, production, distribution and commercialisation,” he said. “There is a strong basis for describing this as a commercial ecosystem of exploitation,” Afridi added. For Zara and many others like her, the consequences of an encounter that began with an online game remain difficult to escape. “I was, and am, scared,” she said. “I live in fear.”

Bodies of 2 FC personnel who went missing in Bannu recovered. BANNU: The bodies of two Frontier Constabulary (FC) personnel who went missing a day earlier were recovered from the Kamali graveyard in Palosi, Rescue 1122 and local sources said on Monday. The deceased personnel were identified as Havaldar Ishaq and Sepoy Umar Hayat. Both belonged to Platoon No 59. According to sources, the personnel were allegedly abducted by unidentified armed men from Saifan Kozi Khel in the Karam Garhi area within the jurisdiction of Cantt police station on Sunday evening. Following the incident, security was tightened in the area, while a search operation for the unidentified assailants was launched. Further investigation was under way, sources said. The incident comes a week after an Elite Force constable was martyred within the jurisdiction of the Bannu Cantonment Police Station. KP witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks in August compared with July, according to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). The province, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent. Deaths resulting from terrorist attacks declined from 69 in July to 44 in August, while injuries declined from 96 to 70, representing a decrease of 27pc.

Oil prices slide on hopes of diplomacy in Iran war. Oil prices slid to their ​lowest in more than a week on Monday as investors hoped for diplomatic progress on the US-Israeli war on Iran due to this ‌week’s UN meeting and eyed a partial recovery in shipments from Saudi Arabia despite ongoing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis. Brent crude futures and US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude touched their lowest since September 10 earlier on Monday. The Brent contract for November was at $102.09 a barrel at 11:55am PKT, down $1.78, or 1.71 per cent, ​after settling 0.91pc lower on Friday. The WTI October contract that is expiring on Tuesday fell $1.97, or 1.96pc, to $98.33 a barrel ​following a 1.58pc drop in the previous session. “It seems that a degree of risk premium is ⁠being removed from oil prices on hopes that a diplomatic path to de-escalate the US-Iran war may arrive this week,” said Tim ​Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. “Whether that hope proves to be warranted or not is another question. Time will tell.” WTI broke ​a key psychological support at $100 a barrel while some investors may have rolled over their positions in the October contract a day ahead of expiry to November, a Singapore-based broker said. Iran and the US exchanged new threats on Sunday, although President Donald Trump said he would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud ​Pezeshkian, who is expected to be in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly. Iran has conveyed its conditions to mediators ​for re-engaging in negotiations aimed at ending the war with the US, Al Jazeera cited Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, as saying in an interview ‌on Saturday. However, ⁠tensions in the Middle East remained elevated as Yemen’s Houthi rebels said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital of Riyadh on Saturday with missiles and drones, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub. On Monday, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), Hossein Mohebbi, said Iran would use new weapons and target locations not previously attacked if the US ​launched a new offensive against ​it, according to the Fars ⁠news agency. China has asked Iran to help rein in the Houthis after an appeal to Beijing by Saudi Arabia following the attacks, according to three Iranian sources familiar with the matter. The attacks by the ​Houthis on Saudi Aramco’s East-West pipeline have prompted the state energy firm to increase exports through the Strait ​of Hormuz this ⁠month and next after halting some shipments via Yanbu. “Middle East oil flows remain surprisingly strong despite the disruption to Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline,” JPMorgan analysts said in a September 18 note , adding that the total oil flows averaged 17.1 million bpd in the past 10 days, just 6.1 ⁠million bpd ​below the 2025 average. “The most notable pivot has come from Saudi Arabia,” the ​analysts said, as satellite data indicated Saudi oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 2.9 million bpd over the past six days, up from just 700,000 ​bpd in August.

Chinese President Xi to visit US from Sept 23-25 for talks with Trump. China’s President Xi Jinping will visit the United States this week for talks with President Donald Trump, Beijing confirmed on Monday. Xi will be there from September 23 to 25 (Wednesday to Friday), a government statement said. Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the two leaders would “have an in-depth exchange of views on major issues concerning China-US relations and world peace and development”. Beijing would “work with the US to enrich the substance of the relationship of constructive strategic stability between China and the US, strengthen dialogue and cooperation, (and) properly manage differences”, he added. Washington had already made clear that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies were due to meet this week, in what is expected to be a bid to ease tensions over trade, technology and broader strategic issues. Trump will personally welcome Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday before their meetings the following day, a US official confirmed. The US leader was welcomed by China’s vice president when he landed in Beijing for his state visit in May. “I’ll be discussing almost everything with him,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday. The simmering trade war between the two countries is a key concern, and the threat of military confrontation over Taiwan looms large as well. While both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year, they have yet to secure a lasting agreement. Vice Premier He Lifeng, China’s top negotiator for trade, is in the US for meetings with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The two discussed creating a communication channel for AI concerns, as they met on Sunday. Trump’s Iran war casts a long shadow too, as China seeks to avoid US sanctions against countries dealing with Tehran, despite reports that Beijing supplied Iran with intelligence for a strike on US troops.

Interior Minister Naqvi warns PTI against Sept 27 protest call, urges party to change course. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday warned PTI against its proposed September 27 long march, urging the party to refrain from proceeding with the protest. He made the statement while addressing a press briefing. Naqvi’s remarks come as the party prepares for a nationwide protest and march towards Islamabad on September 27 to press for the release of its incarcerated founder, Imran Khan. “We have clearly told them (PTI) that they can never achieve anything through such drama, and I will say again that there is still time; they should not go into this situation,” he said, advising the party to “not enter a dead-end street”. Naqvi vowed the government will not “leave any loopholes” in its response if the party went ahead with the protest. The interior minister held that PTI’s majority leadership was not in favour of the march. “[However], if they do, then we have the Islamabad High Court (IHC) order , and the government will ensure its implementation.” He appealed to PTI to adopt a different approach. “Do not harm yourself and your workers,” he said. On being asked if the government had any “long-term solution” to PTI’s frequent protest calls, the interior minister said, “I believe this time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway.” When asked why the government was reluctant to shift PTI founder Imran Khan to a private health facility — as requested by his party and family — amid concerns about his health, the minister said doctors examined Imran last night. “If they demand that his check-up should be done at a hospital, then we did have one last night [..] we are already fulfilling the demand,” Naqvi said. “As for the treatment that is prescribed under the law, we will do everything according to the law. But we will not do it simply because they are demanding it,” the interior minister added. Naqvi, during his talk, contended that PTI’s senior leadership was not in favour of the march. On being asked if the interior ministry will fulfil its role in the upcoming protests, he said, “This time, we will fulfil our role completely. As I said, it will be once and for all.” When asked whether the federal government had any plans to ban the party, the interior minister reiterated, “As I am telling you, this time we will find a once-and-for-all solution. We can’t afford this every time.” Naqvi was also asked if the government was considering imposing governor rule in PTI-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP). At this, the minister said, “Look, we have already made it clear to them that whatever legal options are available, the prime minister, in consultation with our law ministry, will utilise them.” However, he clarified that the party will not be allowed to “come to Islamabad and shut down the city for ten days. That possibility does not exist”. Naqvi also spoke about the creation of new provinces, saying that the matter was progressing rapidly and that public participation in the campaign had increased. He said: “The new provinces issue is moving forward at a pace that we cannot even imagine. The way people are practically coming forward, whether they are chambers, traders or individuals, everyone is playing their role in one way or another. I am very hopeful that, God willing, and if the public wants it, new provinces will certainly be created. “And as far as the movement for new provinces is concerned, I believe it is moving ahead rapidly,” he added. Naqvi’s warning comes as part of the government’s pushback against the party’s proposed march. On Sunday, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the government would not allow any violent group to reach Islamabad or block roads, stressing that the administration would ensure compliance with an IHC order against disruption to public movement. The IHC order, issued on September 14, ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Sunday also warned that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated Rs120 billion loss to the economy each day. Last week, following the IHC judgement , Naqvi warned that the government would stop anyone from marching towards the federal capital “in every possible way”. The development also comes amid reports of a crackdown on PTI workers ahead of the September 27 march.

Two officers among 6 martyred, 8 terrorists killed in Hangu fire exchange: ISPR. Two officers and four others were martyred while eight terrorists were killed in a fire exchange in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Hangu district on Sunday, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said. During an intense fire exchange between a “security forces convoy and Khwarij ”, 23-year-old Captain Abuzar Farooq from Gujranwala and 22-year-old Lieutenant Sheraz Babar of Chakwal, “who were leading their troops from the front, fought gallantly and paid the ultimate sacrifice and embraced martyrdom along with their four men”. According to images released by ISPR, the other four men comprised three sepoys and a “non-combatant”. On the other hand, “eight Khwarij belonging to Indian-sponsored Fitna al Khwarij were sent to hell due to effective engagement by own troops”, the ISPR statement added. The state uses the term Fitna al Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). A sanitisation operation was being conducted to eliminate any other terrorist found in the area, ISPR said. It affirmed that the “relentless counterterrorism campaign under vision ‘Azm-i- Istehkam’ (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”. “These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation at all costs,” the military’s media wing stated. Later in the evening, the funeral prayers of the martyred personnel were offered, following which, their bodies were dispatched to their native towns. Sunday’s development comes two days after a two-pronged assault near a mosque in the old Police Lines of KP’s Kohat district claimed 23 lives, including those of 17 policemen. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. KP witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks in August compared with July, according to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). On August 7, a captain was martyred while seven terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Hangu. On July 30, a deputy superintendent of police (DSP) was among nine cops martyred and 28 others were injured after terrorists attacked the Khazina Banda checkpost in Hangu. Days later, security forces were reported to have killed the mastermind behind the attack.

DPM Dar arrives in New York ahead of UN General Assembly session. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar arrived in New York to participate in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), which will be held from Sept 21 to 25, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Monday. In a post on social media platform X, FO said DPM Dar has a “full programme” of high-level engagements in the week. “He will participate in ministerial forums and deliver Pakistan’s statements and interventions on key issues of importance to Pakistan, including bilateral, regional and international priorities across the UN agenda,” the FO said. Alongside accompanying Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif — who is due to arrive in New York later this week — DPM Dar will hold a series of bilateral meetings with his counterparts and participate in a range of high-level engagements on the sidelines of the UNGA, it added. Upon arriving in New York on Monday, Dar was received by Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, Ambassador to the US Rizwan Saeed Sheikh, Pakistan Consul General in New York Aamer Ahmad Atozai, and officers of Pakistan’s Mission to the UN and Consulate in New York. In a curtain raiser posted on X on Sunday, the FO said that during the visit, Dar will attend the meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Contact Group on Jammu and Kashmir, where he will highlight Pakistan’s “unwavering support” for the right to self-determination for Kashmiris. DPM Dar will also attend several high-level meetings on the Palestine issue, including a meeting of the eight Arab-Islamic countries and a high-level ministerial meeting of the global alliance for the implementation of the two-state solution, among others. According to the FO, DPM Dar is also expected to deliver a statement during the UN Security Council high-level briefing on artificial intelligence. He will also chair a meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation’s Council of Ministers. The Pakistani delegation at the UNGA has been significantly streamlined as part of the government’s austerity measures . Dar and senior foreign-policy adviser Tariq Fatemi will form the core of the prime minister’s delegation. Several federal ministers who were initially expected to travel were dropped from the trip, according to sources at the country’s UN mission.

Detention of Imran's sisters under MPO challenged in LHC. LAHORE: The preventive detention of former prime minister and PTI founder Imran Khan’s three sisters was challenged before the Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday. Earlier today, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were detained for 30 days ahead of the party’s September 27 protest call. The development follows the detention of Imran’s other sister, Aleema Khan, after Lahore Deputy Commissioner (DC) ordered her detention for 30 days on Sunday. Shahraiz Khan, Aleema’s son, filed a petition through Advocate Rana Mudassar Umar, challenging the detention orders issued by the Lahore DC against his mother and two aunts. The petition contends that the DC unlawfully issued the detention orders and failed to follow the procedure prescribed under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance. It argues that the orders contain no specific allegations and demonstrate no application of mind. It also says that ordinary criminal law and less restrictive measures were not considered. The petition further contends that the grounds for detention were not communicated within the required period, alleging that the detention orders were issued after the arrests. It asks the court to set aside the detention orders issued by the Lahore DC and declare them unlawful. The detention has come amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its September 27 countrywide protest and march to Islamabad, which the party has called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. In an order dated Sept 20, a copy of which is available with Dawn , the Lahore DC Office ordered that Noreen and Uzma be detained for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960, stating that the two were “prejudicial to the public safety and maintenance of public order”. Aleema Khan was also detained under a similar order on Sunday. Party’s Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram had accused Punjab police of “arresting both sisters of Imran, along with their children and the sons of Aleema Khan”. Akram claimed that the individuals had “been placed in an armoured vehicle and are being taken to an unknown location”. The detentions come after a string of reported actions against the PTI in Punjab ahead of its September 27 protest. On Sunday, Sahiwal police arrested Asad Khan Baloch, former mayor of the municipal corporation and ex-ticket holder for PTI, along with the party’s city president in Sahiwal, Muhammad Shahid Chohan. PTI also claimed that MNAs Sanaullah Mastikhel , Ahsan Jamal Khan and Mian Ghous were taken into custody, according to the party’s information secretary. However, the government has vowed to stop the march, and the Islamabad High Court (IHC) has ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”.

Pakistan carries out 'calibrated’ airstrikes against terrorist targets in border region with Afghanistan. Pakistan conducted airstrikes on terrorist sites “in the border region with Afghanistan”, killing more than 28 terrorists, the information ministry said on Monday. In a statement, the ministry stressed that the “calibrated” strikes were carried out “against the hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations responsible” for the recent multiple terrorist incidents in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. “Based on credible intelligence, selective targeting of terrorist camps and hideouts belonging to Fitna al Khawarij and its affiliates has also been carried out in the border region with Afghanistan with precision and accuracy,” the statement said. It added: “Three targets were destroyed with precision, including a suicide bombers’ training markaz (centre), killing 28 terrorists alongside multiple suicide bombers. “Large quantities of weapons and ammunition stored at these marakiz (centres) and hideouts were also destroyed.” The state uses the term Fitna al Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Prior to the airstrikes, security forces conducted a “well-planned intelligence-based ground operation” on Sunday against a group of terrorists in KP’s Kohat and Hangu districts, the ministry said. “As a result of precise and skilful engagement, nine khawarij belonging to Indian proxy Fitna al Khawarij were sent to hell, while several were injured,” the statement added. The ministry highlighted that Pakistan had “always strived for the maintenance of peace and stability in the region”. “However, the safety and security of our citizens remains our foremost priority. It is a matter of grave concern that Afghanistan continues to remain a hub of terrorism,” it said, specifying that the “threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan”. “In this context, our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs. Maximum precautions were taken, and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs,” the ministry asserted. The airstrikes come a few days after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. On Sunday, two officers and four others were martyred while eight terrorists were eliminated during a fire exchange between a security forces convoy and armed combatants, the military’s media wing said. There has been a resurgence in terrorism in Pakistan since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from Dec 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA). ‘Ghazab lil Haq under vision Azm-i-Istehkam’ In its Monday statement, the information ministry reaffirmed that the “relentless counterterrorism campaign Ghazab lil Haq under vision ‘ Azm-i-Istehkam ’ by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”. On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts. The last time Pakistan carried out strikes in the border region with Afghanistan was in late June , with the government saying they were in response to a wave of terrorist attacks, including one on a Rangers camp in Karachi . According to Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, 25 terrorists were killed in those strikes in Paktia, Paktika and Kunar. Pakistan had also carried out similar strikes on terrorist hideouts along its border with Afghanistan earlier that month, killing 26 terrorists. In July, security forces responded to unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban at border posts in Kurram, security sources had said. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against TTP and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. Last week, responding to Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid’s remarks , the information ministry had stressed that Pakistan consistently pursued constructive engagement with the Afghan Taliban, but would not allow what it called the “pretence of dialogue” to shield those threatening its people. In his remarks, Mujahid had said Kabul wanted dialogue with Islamabad, but had also warned of “retaliatory action” if Pakistan carried out military operations inside Afghanistan — a warning that the information ministry rejected.

After Aleema, Imran’s sisters Uzma and Noreen also detained in Lahore under MPO for 30 days. Former prime minister and PTI founder Imran Khan’s sisters, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were detained for 30 days on Monday, ahead of the party’s September 27 protest call. The development follows the detention of Imran’s other sister, Aleema Khan, after Lahore’s deputy commissioner (DC) ordered her detention or arrest for 30 days on Sunday. The detention has come amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its September 27 countrywide protest and march to Islamabad, which the party has called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. In an order dated Sept 20, a copy of which is available with Dawn , the Lahore DC Office ordered that Noreen and Uzma be detained for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960, stating that the two were “prejudicial to the public safety and maintenance of public order”. The MPO ordinance allows the authorities to order detention and restrict judicial review of such orders. The two will remain in custody under the superintendent, Central Jail, Kot Lakhpat, it said. The order stated that the two were involved in the May 9 protest and “motivated the workers to damage public and government property”. “Moreover, they are again mobilising the workers through social media and public meetings to create a law and order situation, raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the government/institution in order to provoke and incite them,” the order read. “Accordingly, multiple cases including 96/23 PS Race Course were registered,” it said, stating that Uzma and Noreen were “potential dangers to public peace and tranquillity”. “Such activists will give rise to a situation prejudicial to public safety and maintenance of public order, if left unchecked.” The decision was taken in a meeting held on Sunday, under the chairmanship of the Lahore DC Muhammad Ali Ijaz, where the issue was discussed and members “endorsed” the “evidence” presented by the police. The order stated that the Lahore DC was convinced that Uzma and Noreen’s presence “at any public place will pose a grave threat to the public safety and will likely cause breach of public peace and public order”. In a post on X in the early hours of Monday, the party’s Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram had accused Punjab police of “arresting both sisters of Imran, along with their children and the sons of Aleema Khan”. Akram claimed that the individuals had “been placed in an armoured vehicle and are being taken to an unknown location”. PTI lawyer Awais Younas Chaudhry had confirmed to Dawn that all three of Imran’s sisters had been arrested. “Earlier Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan were confined to their house, but on Monday morning they were taken to an unknown place,” he claimed. PTI, in a post on X, condemned the alleged arrest, calling it a “blatant abuse of authority, a violation of fundamental rights, and an act of political victimisation”. “Such conduct is illegal, unconstitutional, and is condemned in the strongest possible terms,” the party said. Meanwhile, Imran’s son Kasim Khan, in a post on X, alleged that Uzma and Noreen had been “abducted”. “This is a disgrace,” Kasim wrote, claiming that authorities had “broken into my aunties and cousins houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation”. “No reasons for arrest have been stated. No news has been released as to where they have been taken,” he wrote. PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, in a post on X, condemned the detention and stressed that the country did not “need further confrontation, rather an end to political tensions”. Gohar noted that the arrest of “PTI’s parliamentarians and their family members will only exacerbate tensions”. “The state must immediately alter its course of action. We are merely seeking justice and raising our voices for it,” he wrote. Speaking to Dawn , former member of the Punjab Assembly Seemabia Tahir said, “It was unfortunate that the family members [..] were facing such brutality”. She expressed hope that following this, “people will surely come out of their houses on Sept 27”. Aleema’s detention On Sunday, Aleema was detained under similar orders. The September 20 order, a copy of which is available with Dawn , said DC Ijaz had ordered the detention or arrest of Aleema and a man named Muhammad Ameer under the Punjab MPO. Following the arrest, Aleema’s sister Noreen addressed a press conference in Lahore, flanked by her sister’s counsel, Advocate Mudassir Umar. Noreen claimed Aleema was “picked up” along with her driver after she left her residence on Saturday, and they later learnt that Aleema’s vehicle was parked at a police station. Meanwhile, the lawyer said they had yet to receive official confirmation of her arrest. Police sources had confirmed to Dawn on Sunday that Aleema was taken to Lahore’s Kot Lakhpat jail. After Uzma and Noreen were also detained, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja posted on X that in light of “fascist onslaught” in Punjab, particularly Lahore, an organising committee had been formed for the Lahore district to run the party’s matter “through consultation and agreement”. He added that consultations would be held with parliamentarians in Punjab on Monday and Tuesday. He also shared a statement notifying the constitution of the committee. The statement said, ““The organising committee shall have complete authority to take all actions and devise and implement all plans for the better functioning of the affairs of the party in the Lahore district.” Former lawmaker Malik Zaheer Abbas has been appointed as the committee’s convener and the body also compises Haroon Akbar, Asghar Gujjar, Awais Anjum, Yasir Gillani and Amir Qureshi. Detentions ahead of Sept 27 protest The detentions of Imran’s sisters come after a string of reported actions against the PTI in Punjab ahead of its September 27 protest. On Sunday, Sahiwal police arrested Asad Khan Baloch, former mayor of the municipal corporation and ex-ticket holder for PTI, along with the party’s city president in Sahiwal, Muhammad Shahid Chohan. PTI also claimed that MNAs Sanaullah Mastikhel , Ahsan Jamal Khan and Mian Ghous were taken into custody, according to the party’s information secretary. District authorities had also issued preventive detention orders against dozens of PTI workers under MPO a week ago, including 31 in one Punjab notification and a further 14 in Toba Tek Singh. Similar reports have come from Islamabad, where the PTI plans to march on the protest day. However, the government has vowed to stop the march, and the Islamabad High Court (IHC) has ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”.

AI safety paradox. ANTHROPIC chief Dario Amodei wants the companies building the world’s most powerful artificial intelligence to slow down. Not stop, but slow the advance of frontier capabilities enough for safety and security work to catch up. He calls it “pacing the frontier”. Amodei says two things have changed. AI is beginning to help build the next generation of AI, raising the possibility of recursive self-improvement. At the same time, frontier agents have started doing things during testing that their developers did not expect or authorise. Then came Jacob Coxon. The Anthropic resear­cher, who had previously worked at OpenAI, resigned before his equity vested and accused the industry of “gambling with our lives”. His fear that increasingly autonomous systems could threaten humanity before the end of the decade is not a scientific forecast. What makes Coxon important is where the warning comes from, ie, someone who worked inside two laboratories closest to the frontier. There is, however, an uncomfortable irony in Big Tech sounding the alarm. Anthropic is not standing outside this economy warning everyone else about it. In 2025, it accepted a two-year Pentagon agreement with a $200 million ceiling to develop AI capabilities for US national security. It built Claude Gov for classified environments and says its systems support intelligence analysis, operational planning, and cyber operations. Anthropic says it later refused demands that would have removed its restrictions around mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. The contradiction is that companies warning that powerful AI may become difficult to control are simultaneously moving it deeper into military and intelligence systems. AI regulators should operate transparently and remain subject to judicial oversight. The contradiction goes beyond Anthropic. An Associated Press investigation found commercial Microsoft and OpenAI technology being used by the Israeli military in Gaza and Lebanon, including in intelligence systems connected to targeting. Microsoft later said its review found no evidence that its technology had been used to harm civilians. AI is already being folded into warfare while the debate about what these systems may become is still taking shape. Anthropic’s own threat reporting makes the concern more concrete. The company says it has disrupted attempts to use Claude for cyber operations, surveillance, conventional weapons development, and biological misuse. The more revealing incidents came during safety testing. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models in cyber evaluations circumvented isolation controls, reached the internet, and compromised parts of OpenAI’s own research infrastructure and systems belonging to Hugging Face. Anthropic initially disclosed three cases in which Claude models gained unauthorised access to real third-party systems during evaluations and later identified a fourth. None of this means an AI has suddenly become conscious or malicious. The immediate problem is scale. A capable hacker, weapons engineer or surveillance operation needs expertise, time and people. AI can lower those barriers, work at machine speed, and let one operator run several specialised agents at once. Capabilities once concentrated in governments or specialist organisations could become cheaper and easier to reproduce. Amodei’s answer is to give independent evaluators permanent, employee-like access to frontier laboratories and their safety processes. He also wants companies to coordinate around common standards and eventually some form of international agreement. Questions, however, remain as to who chooses the evaluators. Who pays? What can they publish? And what happens if an evaluator says a model is unsafe and the company releases it anyway? Amodei points to organisations such as METR, an independent nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI systems for dangerous capabilities and loss of control risks. METR says it takes no funding from frontier AI companies or donations directed by their employees, although those companies provide substantial free access to models. But an evaluator can test and warn. Unless someone can act on those findings, the final decision remains with the company. Meta offers a useful precedent. Its Oversight Board was designed to operate at arm’s length, and its decisions on individual content cases bind Meta. Its wider policy recommendations do not. In 2025, the board criticised Meta for making major moderation changes without publicly demonstrating adequate human rights due diligence. However, it lacked enforcement power. The bottom line is, independent oversight is great. It can improve accountability but will not necessarily shift ultimate power. Thus, my argument isn’t against self-regulation. AI is moving too quickly for governments to understand every capability before it appears, and companies can impose safeguards faster than legislatures can pass laws. But voluntary restraint cannot be the final layer of accountability. Politics makes even that difficult. Donald Trump has made American AI leadership part of his competition with China and has dismissed the latest safety alarm, arguing that slowing development would benefit Beijing. Whether China is actually better placed to win that competition is a larger question, and one I am leaving for another piece. The point here is simpler: commercial competition and geopolitics reward speed at precisely the moment some of the people building these systems are asking for caution. Regulation is necessary, but it carries its own dangers. Rules written largely by AI companies could entrench the biggest firms. Rules written too broadly by governments could turn ‘AI safety’ into an excuse for censorship, surveillance or control over legitimate research and speech. A better approach would be risk-based. Low-risk applications need little intervention, while systems crossing defined thresholds in areas such as cyber capability, biological risk, weapons, critical infrastructure or autonomous action should face much tougher requirements. Frontier models could undergo mandatory independent testing before deployment, serious incidents should be disclosed, and companies should retain liability for foreseeable harms. Evaluators need protected funding, and whistleblowers need legal safeguards. Regulators should operate transparently and remain subject to judicial oversight. Most importantly, the rules should target dangerous capabilities and conduct, not political viewpoints or lawful expression. The difficult question is no longer whether AI needs oversight. Even some of the people building the most powerful systems now say it does. The challenge is designing rules strong enough to matter without giving either corporations or governments powers that create a different kind of danger. The writer is the founder of Media Matters for Democracy. Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026
