They should encourage states that are vulnerable to U.S. pressure to stay the course and do what they can to buttress the Court’s resiliency. At a practical level, countries could offer basic banking services to ICC officials who have been targeted by U.S. sanctions. Member states should also use their negotiations of the annual General Assembly resolution on the ICC, scheduled to take place between October and November, to drum up public support for its work and galvanise pushback against the U.S. attack on this pillar of the international justice architecture. 7. Recalibrating UN operations in Myanmar Myanmar’s installation of a nominally civilian administration in April, following elections stage-managed by the military four months earlier, has created a dilemma for the UN. The elections have not restored state authority or legitimacy, and Naypyitaw does not have a credible strategy for ending the country’s armed conflict, either through negotiation or military victory. 130 Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°188, Myanmar’s New Administration: Military Consolidation, Not Transition , 3 June 2026. Humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate as fighting, economic decline and fear of conscription grip the country. 131 “ Myanmar Humanitarian Update no. 51 ”, UN OCHA, 9 March 2026. Even so, more of Myanmar’s regional neighbours are giving the new administration de facto recognition, with Min Aung Hlaing – the coup leader who is now president – recently visiting India, China, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Beijing maintains a firm position limiting discussion of Myanmar at the UN, while Secretary-General Guterres has shown little willingness to invest political capital in the issue. Absent new diplomatic momentum in the near term, UN officials will need to calibrate engagement carefully to reduce harm, sustain livelihoods and support development without conferring legitimacy on abusive forms of rule. Much of this work will fall to the new UN leadership in Yangon. In October 2025, Guterres appointed veteran official Gwyn Lewis as resident and humanitarian coordinator ad interim, ending the ineffective practice of rotating the position among agency heads. 132 Lewis has the ad interim designation because the Secretary-General does not want to acknowledge the authorities politically by writing to seek their agreement to the appointment. See Crisis Group Special Briefing N°12, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2024-2025 , 10 September 2024. The resident coordinator will need to shape the UN’s engagement with the new administration while ensuring the organisation can continue delivering essential humanitarian and development assistance. Just as importantly, the office should provide clear strategic direction to the whole UN country team so that agencies operate according to a consistent approach within current political constraints. UN officials will also need to manage relations with Myanmar’s ethnic armed groups. Aid agencies already deliver assistance in parts of the country outside state control, working through local partners despite the absence of formal agreements with Naypyitaw. As the devastating March 2025 earthquake showed, the UN remains one of the few organisations capable of delivering international aid at scale to civilians in much of the country, including areas outside government control. 133 Richard Horsey, “ Support Vital for Myanmar’s Quake Victims, Despite Military Obstacles ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 1 April 2025; “ End of Mission Report United Nations Disaster Assessment & Coordination – Earthquake 7.7M Response – Myanmar (29Mar-16Apr 2025) ”, UN OCHA, 23 February 2026; “ First person: Myanmar aid workers brave conflict and harsh conditions to bring aid to earthquake victims ”, UN, 30 April 2025. The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank have become the largest and most consistent providers of assistance to Myanmar’s people, but they rightly cannot channel funds through a government they do not recognise. Their support is therefore delivered off-budget – outside state systems – and depends on UN agencies for fiduciary oversight and distribution. The resident coordinator will need to mind the political sensitivities of the UN role in providing this support, as well as the differing approaches of neighbouring states – including Bangladesh, China, India and Thailand – toward informal cross-border assistance. 134 Thomas Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 8 July 2026; Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°186, Fractured Heartland: Shan Politics and Conflict in Post-coup Myanmar , 27 November 2025. The next Secretary-General will have an opportunity to reset the UN’s overall strategy [in Myanmar] and provide stronger political backing for the envoy. The same balancing act applies to the UN’s diplomatic track. Special Envoy Julie Bishop, who has struggled to translate her high-level regional access into meaningful entry points for UN diplomacy, has burned most of her bridges with Myanmar’s leaders by taking an increasingly strident public line – for example, returning from Naypyitaw to tell UN member states in June that the election was designed to entrench military rule and that Min Aung Hlaing’s proposed 100-day peace plan inspires no confidence. 135 “Special Envoy on Myanmar’s remarks to the General Assembly”, UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, 19 June 2026. The next Secretary-General will have an opportunity to reset the UN’s overall strategy and provide stronger political backing for the envoy. 136 The envoy role was mandated by the UN General Assembly in December 2017 to support UN engagement on a range of political priorities. “ Situation of human rights in Myanmar ”, UN General Assembly, UN Doc. A/RES/72/248, 23 January 2018. An important test will come at the UN General Assembly. Since the 2021 coup, China and the U.S. have informally maintained the status quo by leaving in place the incumbent ambassador, Kyaw Moe Tun, who was appointed by the elected government and later aligned himself with the parallel National Unity Government. Naypyitaw is expected to press its case to have its nominee recognised as Myanmar’s permanent representative when the Credentials Committee meets in November. China committed in a 17 June statement with Min Aung Hlaing in Beijing to support Myanmar’s “full, equal and constructive participation” at the UN, repeating this formula in the General Assembly two days later. 137 “ Joint Statement of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the People’s Republic of China on Accelerating the Building of a China – Myanmar Community with a Shared Future (17 June 2026) ”, Republic of the Union of Myanmar, 18 June 2026; and informal meeting of the General Assembly plenary convened to hear the Special Envoy’s briefing on Myanmar, 19 June 2026. It is unclear what diplomatic capital Beijing may expend to this end. A decision has been put off each year because the permanent members who sit on the Credentials Committee – China, the U.S. and Russia – have preferred the status quo to a divisive vote, and because any consideration of the competing credentials for Myanmar could prompt a similar debate about the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan. 138 The Committee, appointed at the General Assembly’s first plenary meeting under rule 28, met once in the 80th session, on 25 November 2025. Its report proposed a single postponement of the competing credentials for both Myanmar and Afghanistan, adopted without a vote. See “Report of the Credentials Committee”, A/80/547, 25 November 2025, paras 8 to 10, approved by the General Assembly on 12 December 2025 (Resolution 80/114). The credentials debate could coincide with the International Court of Justice’s expected ruling in the genocide case against Myanmar that was filed by The Gambia. 139 Public hearings in The Gambia v. Myanmar case closed at the International Court of Justice on 29 January 2026, and judgment is pending. The Court will rule both on whether Myanmar committed genocide and on whether it failed to prevent and punish genocidal acts. A finding that Myanmar committed genocide would be the first time the Court has held a state responsible for such a crime. In the two previous genocide judgments, Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro and Croatia v. Serbia , the Court found a failure to prevent and punish in the first and no proven specific intent in the second. See “The concluding stage of The Gambia v. Myanmar genocide case before the International Court of Justice”, Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect, 10 February 2026. Although the case’s outcome remains uncertain, a finding of state responsibility arriving at the same time as a credentials dispute would intensify international divisions over the issue of the Myanmar administration’s legitimacy. It would also narrow even further the UN’s room for manoeuvre in Myanmar, since Naypyitaw would view it with even more antagonism. The cost for regional leaders of associating with Min Aung Hlaing might rise as well, complicating high-level visits to the country though probably not turning the tide on diplomatic normalisation. The UN does not have the leverage to achieve major change in Myanmar. But the organisation is crucial for delivering humanitarian and other support to vulnerable civilians. A credible operational strategy, backed by sustained political support from headquarters, will therefore remain essential to efforts to alleviate public hardship and the effects of armed conflict. 8. Protecting the UN’s gender work in conflict settings The UN’s reform agenda has raised thorny issues about how the institution should organise its work to support women and girls. In late 2025, Secretary-General Guterres proposed merging the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) with UN Women as part of the UN80 initiative. 140 Other proposed mergers under UN80 include combining the UN Development Programme and the UN Office for Project Services; the UN Institute for Training and Research and the UN System Staff College; and the World Health Organisation and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS. UNFPA leads the UN’s work on sexual and reproductive health, while UN Women (approximately one third the size of UNFPA) advocates for normative shifts on gender issues, including the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda, and distributes funding to NGOs for related programming. 141 With an annual budget of $1.53 billion, UNFPA’s model focuses on service delivery through 3,569 staff in 150 countries. “ As-Is Analysis: A Baseline for the UNFPA - UN Women Strategic Merger Assessment ”, UN80 Initiative, Work Package 4, Working Document, 6 March 2026. Whether the merger will come to pass is not clear. Amid aid cuts and pushback against gender equality worldwide, many member states and UN officials worry that combining these entities would hobble the UN’s work on gender, including efforts to support women and girls affected by conflict, for years to come. The Secretary-General’s proposal included a request for a UN-prepared report (published in March) that evaluated the risks and benefits of a merger – an idea that had been discussed and discarded in 2023. 142 Member states and UN officials report a sense that, whatever its findings, the study was meant to recommend a merger because the Secretary-General and Deputy Secretary-General wished to show that they were serious about making large-scale reforms to make the UN more efficient. For more, see “ Independent Review of the UN System’s Capacity to Deliver on Gender Equality ”, Dalberg, 11 February 2023. The merger it proposed would bring together UNFPA and UN Women in a new entity with a unified voice. It would also save the UN between $32 and $38 million per year, which the UN would urge member states to reinvest in the new entity’s work. 143 “ Preliminary Findings from the Strategic Merger Assessment of UNFPA and UN Women ”, UN80 Initiative, 30 March 2026. The assessment acknowledged, but did not suggest ways to mitigate, the risk that member states could eliminate important but contentious areas of work – including a number of sexual and reproductive health services and work on LGBTQI+ protections – during negotiations to create the new entity. 144 Given that the U.S. has been spearheading the pressure on the Secretary-General and his deputy to show their willingness to streamline the UN, combined with U.S. positions against the UN’s gender equality and WPS, many member states and UN officials point out that this merger proposal is like offering the U.S. a prime opportunity to weaken the UN’s gender work for years to come, by opening a negotiation on a new mandate where no negotiation or new mandate is necessary or desirable. [The] separate mandates [of UN Women and UNFPA] help the UN respond to distinct political, security and humanitarian issues. There are other risks, too. Though both agencies work on gender issues in conflict-affected countries, their separate mandates help the UN respond to distinct political, security and humanitarian issues. 145 In 2025, UNFPA was active in efforts to ameliorate 50 humanitarian crises, while in 2024 UN Women was working in 43. See “ 2026 Humanitarian Action Overview ”, UNFPA, April 2026; and “ Humanitarian Action Annual Report 2024”, UN Women, 2025. In Afghanistan, for example, UNFPA runs programs including menstrual health education and support for midwives, all in compliance with Taliban edicts. 146 “ Youth centre provides life-changing menstrual hygiene information and supplies to Afghan girls ”, UNFPA Afghanistan, 28 May 2026. Though interactions between the Taliban and UNFPA personnel are sometimes “tense”, the authorities recognise the need for the agency’s services. 147 Crisis Group interview, UN official, New York, July 2026. UN Women’s Afghanistan office is on shakier ground. The Taliban consider UN Women to be among their loudest critics and reject the agency’s frequent calls for repealing highly restrictive decrees as interference in Afghanistan’s internal affairs. 148 Mohammad Farshad Daryosh, “ Potzel criticizes bans on women, girls in Afghanistan ”, Tolo News, 8 March 2023; “ IEA-MOFA statement regarding SRSG briefing to UNSC ”, press release, 22 June 2023. While UN Women supports livelihood projects that the Taliban see as consistent with their goals of keeping the economy afloat and help the agency maintain an in-country presence, its normative positions are a persistent source of friction. Combining the two UN entities may have the effect of imputing these positions to UNFPA and create unnecessary risks for the latter. 149 “ Empowering Afghan Women and Energizing Economies ”, UN Women Afghanistan, 2025. UN efforts to support more than one million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar living in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, also show why keeping UN Women and UNFPA separate is helpful in providing support for women and girls affected by conflict. 150 Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, op. cit. UNFPA offers health services in response to prevalent sexual violence and high pregnancy rates. It must be politically adroit in its engagement with Bangladeshi authorities, given local sensitivities around sexual and reproductive health. 151 Crisis Group telephone interview, humanitarian health practitioner, 25 June 2024. See also Cristal Downing, “ Amid Aid Cuts, a Renewed U.S. Policy Increases Health Risks for Women and Girls in Conflict Areas ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 3 March 2025. By contrast, UN Women supports women refugees (including through vocational training) and is involved in politically complex conversations with Dhaka about supporting eventual refugee return to Myanmar. 152 Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, op. cit. Currently, the conversations about health care and political matters are separate, so if the two need to raise their issues with authorities at similar times they can do so separately – even if in coordination – without having to choose one topic over the other. UN officials worry that the appointment of a single UN interlocutor to coordinate with the authorities on both immediate humanitarian priorities and longer-term political objectives could pit the new organisation’s teams against each other when deciding which issues should take higher priority in senior-level engagement. 153 The merger assessment considers this single interlocutor model to be a strength of the proposal, but UN officials consider it a weakness because of the potential trade-offs that would have to be made internally when deciding the priorities to be addressed in government engagement. Crisis Group interviews, UN officials, January-July 2026. Member states across the geographic and political spectrum have expressed concerns about the proposed merger. A coalition including Canada, Poland, South Korea and Sweden – which includes top contributors to both agencies – wrote to the Secretary-General saying they were “not in a position to support such a proposal” given the lack of clarity on how the two mandates could be safeguarded. 154 Canada letter to the UN Secretary-General , 15 May 2026. Separately, Russia and China also emphasised the need to protect the two mandates, albeit voicing different concerns. Russia pointed out that member states have no agreed-upon definition of “sexual rights”, saying it is therefore “inappropriate” for the proposed new entity to work in this domain. China, for its part, stressed that the process of merging two entities should be member state-led and transparent, suggesting that it objected to how the recommendation came about. 155 For more, see Letter from Russia to the UN Secretary-General , UNGA A/80/710, 20 April 2026; Remarks by China on the UN80 initiative , 8 June 2026. In response to requests from member state governing boards for alternative proposals, UN Women and UNFPA distributed their own papers, first in June and then in August, suggesting ways to align some of their work without a merger, including through shared data analytics and joint projects on gender-based violence in some locations. 156 The second of these papers also went into further detail on the costs of a merger, including the initial four-year financial impact ranging from a $9.9 million loss to a $38.2 million gain, after which savings could reach $35.1 million, depending on transition costs and organisational design. According to the UN’s own assessment of the merger, savings would be reinvested in the new entity. “ Further evidence and analysis on both the merger scenario and on alternative options to enhance alignment, impact and efficiency”, UN Women/UNFPA, 7 August 2026. Member states and UN officials should consider whether these proposals would satisfy the desire to increase efficiency without risking the mandate dilution implied by a merger. In so doing, they should shy away from politically ill-timed proposals that would threaten hard-won gains and could weaken UN support for women and girls in conflict and other crises in the long term. 9. Recasting discussions of the future of UN peace operations Diplomats routinely cite peace operations as one of the UN’s flagship contributions to peace and security. But the Security Council has not authorised a large-scale blue helmet force for over a decade, and the number of troops and police personnel serving under the organisation’s banner has halved in the same period. There have also been few new UN Special Political Missions (SPMs), which are solely or largely civilian in nature. As noted in the introduction, the Trump administration has pushed for budget cuts to UN missions of all kinds, questioning their expense, efficiency and apparent lack of concrete goals. To guide discussions about how to revitalise this atrophying tool, the Secretary-General published a review of all forms of peace operations. 157 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations: report of the Secretary General ”, UN General Assembly A/80/798 – UN Security Council S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. The review came out in August, having originally been requested by member states in late 2024. Though this study covers political missions – and makes a strong pitch for the UN to reinvest in prevention and good offices, discussed in the next section – many of its more technical recommendations are specific to operations with military and police components. A number of UN members, including the U.S., have complained that it says nothing startlingly new. 158 See, for example, “ The future of United Nations peace operations: Implementation of the recommendations of the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/70/357 – UNSC S/2015/682, 2 September 2015; “ Declaration of Shared Commitments on UN Peacekeeping Operations ”, UN Secretary-General, 16 August 2018; “ The Pact For The Future ”, UN General Assembly A/RES/79/1, 22 September 2024, paras 42(a)-42(g); “ Chair’s Summary – UN Peacekeeping Ministerial 2025 ”, 14 May 2025. But it is a solid overview of the challenges facing UN operations and a starting point for diplomatic discussions of solving them. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. The report’s diagnosis of the problems facing peace operations is hard to dispute. As it notes, the UN is often tasked with propping up weak ceasefires and political processes amid endemic violence. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. A divided and distracted Security Council provides limited political support for UN personnel on the ground and does not update their mandates in a timely fashion when they encounter changing threats (Council diplomats admit this judgment is fair). 159 “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,137th Meeting of the UN Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10137, 15 April 2026. The Secretary-General stakes out a series of sensible, albeit technocratic, responses to these issues. He suggests that the Security Council should direct UN operations to find political approaches to ending and mitigating conflict; work out “compacts” with states defining shared commitments to making missions work; and take a flexible approach to reviewing and revising mandates. His paper calls for a further Secretariat report examining the capabilities UN missions need to become more agile, while hammering home the need for missions to become more cost-effective and accountable for their performance. UN staffers and diplomats will spend much of the year ahead following up on these proposals, but even if they can fix some of the process issues, broader political questions about the future of UN peace operations will remain. In today’s fraught geopolitical environment, the space for mediators – hailing from the UN or elsewhere – to craft sustainable peace processes will likely remain limited. 160 Crisis Group Briefing, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Security , op. cit. Embattled governments in regions such as the Sahel and countries like Haiti want international forces to neutralise their opponents rather than coax them to the negotiating table. Guterres and most UN officials agree that as a rule the UN should not become directly involved in peace enforcement, even if the Security Council backs ad hoc missions like the GSF in Haiti that the UN system can support logistically and administratively. The fundamental challenge facing the UN is to rebuild a case for conflict parties and other actors to invest in mediation processes and peacebuilding efforts that minimise violence, and that UN peace operations are qualified to offer these efforts support when useful. There may be an audience for this argument. As Crisis Group has noted, efforts to crush insurgencies through force alone in cases such as the Sahel have gone awry. 161 Crisis Group Africa Report N°314, Northern Mali: Returning to Dialogue , 20 February 2024; Crisis Group Africa Report N°321, Understanding JNIM’s Expansion Beyond the Sahel , 20 February 2026; Crisis Group Briefing, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Security , op. cit. While the UN still has a lot of work to do improving how peace operations work, Guterres leaves them with a helpful to-do list. The next Secretary-General’s overarching challenge will be restoring the organisation’s standing as an actor that can deploy peace operations to backstop other peace initiatives when they show promise. 10. Repositioning the Secretary-General’s approach to crisis management When the next Secretary-General takes office on 1 January 2027, she or he will have a brief window of opportunity to overhaul the UN Secretariat’s strategy-making and crisis response mechanisms. Incoming UN leaders typically shake up their executive offices in their first months and table broader proposals for reorganising the Secretariat for member states to consider. 162 Thomas Weiss and Tatiana Carayannis, “ Windows of Opportunity for UN Reform: Historical Insights for the Next Secretary-General ”, International Affairs , vol. 93, no. 2 (2017). In the course of selecting a new Secretary-General, member states have emphasised that the winner should concentrate on peace and security. Many candidates have promised to engage on crisis diplomacy personally, a point emphasised in Guterres’ review of all forms of peace operations. 163 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations: report of the Secretary General ”, op. cit., paras 24-29. But it is necessary to improve the institution’s systems for generating policy options for dealing with new and persistent conflicts, which have grown rusty in recent years. They will also have to prepare for the fall-out of global risks like the El Niño climate pattern on conflict affected states, which will test the diplomatic, humanitarian and development arms of the UN system. Though Secretary-General Guterres made streamlining the UN’s peace and security pillar an early priority, organisational glitches have proliferated on his watch. 164 For more, see proposed budget for 2018-2019 related to the peace and security reform , UNGA A/72/772, 1 March 2018. Guterres has kept a tight grip on decision-making. Officials dealing with peace operations and political affairs, whether in New York or around the world, often feel out of the loop. As crises have proliferated, senior decision-makers in the Secretariat have become debilitatingly cautious, and inter-departmental turf wars (a perennial feature of life at the UN) have festered. Security Council members complain that when they ask for options papers from the Secretary-General – as they have done in cases including Gaza, Sudan, Haiti and Lebanon – the results come slowly and are generally mediocre at best. 165 Forti, “ Prioritising Peace: What the UN Should Ask of Its Next Secretary-General ”, op. cit. UN officials agree that a high priority for the next Secretary-General is to sort out [the] option-generating and decision-making mess. UN officials agree that a high priority for the next Secretary-General is to sort out this option-generating and decision-making mess. Some believe it is a matter of a change in culture (and, in some cases, personnel). Others argue that it is necessary to centralise the UN’s systems for producing options and crisis coordination in a new planning cell inside the Secretary-General’s office, to speed up the process of responding to new conflicts and Security Council requests for help. The next Secretary-General would be well advised to resolve this top-level wiring issue – which will require fairly slight budgetary and managerial effort – before embarking on any wider reform of the Secretariat’s Departments of Peace Operations and Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, which will require more extensive inter-governmental negotiations, and more battles over turf. The new Secretary-General’s choice of senior officials dealing with peace and security will also come under scrutiny. The veto powers typically insist on inserting nominees to run significant departments, often as bargains during the final stages of choosing the Secretary-General. An unwritten division among the major powers has emerged: France fills the post of Under Secretary-General for Peace Operations, the U.S. takes political affairs, the UK deals with humanitarian affairs, China handles economic and social affairs, and Russia names the head of the Office of Counter-terrorism. UN officials and other member states grumble about this carve-up, but successive Secretaries-General have concluded that it is a political necessity to gain support from the Council’s permanent members. 166 Thant Myint-U, “ The Next Secretary-General, Secretariat Reform and the Vexed Question of Senior Appointments ”, NYU Center on International Cooperation, 11 April 2016. Some Secretariat staff worry that the Trump administration will lobby for a hardline loyalist to oversee the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, undermining the Secretary-General’s authority. While it may not be possible to ignore the veto powers entirely, however, both Guterres and his predecessor Ban Ki-moon were able to resist appointing nominees from Washington, Paris and London whom they deemed unsuitable. 167 Ben Donaldson and Fred Carver, “ Backroom Deals: The trade in promises for support between member states and candidates for UN Secretary-General ”, 1 for 8 Billion/Platforma CIPÓ, June 2026. To show at least a modicum of autonomy, the next Secretary-General should follow suit, potentially asking the veto powers for informal shortlists of candidates for particular roles. Equally or more importantly, she or he should look for strong appointees from non-veto capitals to fill key posts in the executive office – including Deputy Secretary-General, Chief of Staff and Political Director – who can buttress top-level decision-making and help balance the influence of P5 proxies in internal debates. 168 Daniel Safran-Hon, “ The Next Secretary-General’s First Decision: Who Runs the 38th Floor? ”, IPI Global Observatory, 13 May 2026. These senior officials could take on direct mediation roles as well. 169 Daniel Safran-Hon, “ UN Peacemaking Needs More Diplomats, Not More Doctrine ”, IPI Global Observatory, 26 August 2026. For all the qualities of her or his advisers, the Secretary-General will also need to get personally involved directly in conflict prevention efforts and peace processes. The new Secretary-General’s team will need to set up a series of early visits for the boss to key capitals in various regions so that she or he can signal that the UN is reinvesting in the business of conflict management. Whereas Guterres was discouraged by early failures in his peacemaking efforts, his successor should embrace a more persistent attitude toward the UN’s role in peacemaking. In the years ahead, the organisation’s biggest failure may not be to fall short of lofty expectations in crisis diplomacy, but to eschew engagement altogether. 170 Richard Gowan and Daniel Forti, “ Make the U.N. great again: The uphill struggle facing the next Secretary General ”, Time , 22 August 2026. IV. Conclusion The UN’s fortunes over the next twelve months will depend in no small part on who its members select as the next Secretary-General. She or he will face considerable pressure to hit the ground running and deliver quick wins for an organisation whose credibility has waned. Doing so will require the expenditure of limited political capital on a range of priorities. Member states will no doubt push the next UN chief to translate their vision for the organisation into plans for its peace and security, development and human rights pillars. The new Secretary-General will also be tasked with stabilising the organisation’s wobbling finances and spearheading a reform agenda. If the past year at the UN was defined by transition, then the coming year may be shaped by how quickly its new leader can deliver. But the next Secretary-General cannot mend all that is fraying at the UN without renewed support from its members. At a moment of worsening geopolitical competition, a more pragmatic approach may be for states to come to a more limited interpretation of the UN’s role in world affairs. Central to that vision would be the organisation’s potential as platform to reduce global risks through communication and deconfliction, rebuilding its credibility as a peacemaker, and helping alleviate the worst of civilian suffering. The organisation will surely also have a role to play in helping the most vulnerable weather global economic shocks, including those linked both to conflict (as in the case of a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz) and to other drivers (such as the El Niño climate pattern). Much of the debate about the UN’s work over the past year has centred on its shortcomings. That focus is understandable considering the worrying state of the international order. But as this briefing has shown, there are many crises where the UN is the only multilateral body with the mandate, legitimacy and capacity to open space for diplomacy. The organisation’s next leader would be wise to double down on those virtues. It may be an imperfect construction of the UN’s role in world affairs, but it is nonetheless an essential one. The Houthis’ Advance to Bab al-Mandab: Has Yemen’s War Returned? eschelhaas Wed, 09/16/2026 - 17:32 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List The Houthis’ Advance to Bab al-Mandab: Has Yemen’s War Returned? Online Event Tuesday, 22 September 2026 10am Washington, DC | 4pm Brussels | 5pm Sanaa Please register here if you would like to attend this online event. Over the past week, the Houthis have swept down Yemen’s western coast and reached Bab al-Mandab, unravelling a defensive line that had held for years, and exposing just how fragmented the government camp’s forces had become. A string of retreats was decisive, as the National Resistance, Giants Brigades and other nominally allied units, each with its own command and backers, lost Khokha, Mokha and the roads linking Taiz, Hodeida and the coast, fighting side by side but never as one army. A foothold near one of the world’s busiest shipping chokepoints gives the Houthis fresh leverage over Saudi Arabia, just as Riyadh’s containment strategy is under strain. It also ties their campaign more closely to Iran’s entrenched standoff with Washington: any disruption to shipping through Bab al-Mandab would compound the effects of restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz, raising the economic costs of a wider confrontation. In this online event, Crisis Group brings together leading experts to discuss how the front collapsed so quickly, what the new balance of power means for Taiz, Marib and the other fronts still in play, and whether Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government and Yemen’s neighbours can keep this round of fighting from sliding into a wider war. Panellists: April Longley Alley | Senior Fellow, The Washington Institute Ahmed Nagi | Senior Analyst, Yemen, Crisis Group Peter Salisbury | Adjunct Professor, Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs Moderator: Yasmine Farouk | Project Director, Gulf and Arabian Peninsula, Crisis Group The panel discussion will be held in English and will be live-streamed on YouTube . 0 0

A Pivotal Moment in Uniting Post-Assad Syria eschelhaas Thu, 09/17/2026 - 12:17 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Syrian President Ahmed Al-Shara, right, and Syrian Democratic Forces commander Mazloum Abdi, left, attend a session at the presidential palace in Damascus. Rami Alsayed / NurPhoto / via AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 17 September 2026 15 minutes A Pivotal Moment in Uniting Post-Assad Syria The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which long enjoyed de facto autonomy in north-eastern Syria, have dissolved. But tensions in the region remain high as talks about integration with the central state proceed. Further compromise would set a useful precedent for other parts of the country. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Syria The scene on 25 August, like countless others in Syria of late, would have been unimaginable a mere two years ago. Mazloum Abdi, commander-in-chief of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), the Kurdish-led group that had autonomously run much of the country’s north east for some fourteen years, stood in Damascus beside the flag of Syria’s former opposition and new state, announcing the SDF’s dissolution and taking on the role of adviser to President Ahmad al-Sharaa. Beyond marking Abdi’s transition to senior government official, the event represented a pivotal moment in the process aimed at integrating the SDF’s institutions into the Syrian state. Damascus and the SDF leadership have come a long way since their troops clashed in early 2026, but difficult questions lie ahead as they continue talks to define the next phase of integration. Deepening cooperation – and providing further clarity to address Syrian Kurds’ concerns about their security and role in governance – is the best way forward. Progress amid Frustration While it has made important progress, the SDF integration process has also been bumpy, generating its fair share of frustrations. Disappointment is particularly acute among the group’s core Kurdish constituency: the deal reached in late August is the latest in a series of compromises leaving the north east far less autonomy than it had enjoyed during most of Syria’s civil war. The shortfall is due partly to the dramatic shift in U.S. policy following the fall of former President Bashar al-Assad’s Baathist regime, as Washington embraced al-Sharaa’s government and wound down its decade-long partnership with the SDF. But the SDF’s own miscalculations also played a role. After agreeing with Damascus in March 2025 to define integration arrangements by year’s end, it dragged its feet. That strategy proved ill-advised. Government forces pressed their advantage on the battlefield in January, and the SDF saw its hand weaken. Tensions prompted by this confrontation linger to this day. Still, the integration process has proven successful in several key respects. It ended weeks of armed conflict that, just nine months ago, threatened to plunge northern Syria into further violence along ethnic lines; secured unprecedented Syrian government commitments to Kurdish rights; enabled the return of thousands of Kurdish families to their homes after years of displacement, partially reversing war-induced demographic changes; and improved prospects for separate talks in neighbouring Türkiye that aim to end decades of insurgency by the Kurdistan Workers Party or PKK, with which the SDF has deep ties. Scepticism of integration runs deep among Kurds, even as prominent Arab voices call for accelerating it. The SDF’s official dissolution marks the beginning of a new, critical phase. Important gaps between the sides remain, notably over the degree to which former SDF-aligned institutions can maintain coherence as they become part of state structures. The parties will also have to contend with countervailing popular pressures in the north east – scepticism of integration runs deep among Kurds, even as prominent Arab voices call for accelerating it. Unrest following the killing of a Kurdish soldier on 10 September has deepened the polarisation. If Damascus and the former SDF leadership can address these issues together, they could simultaneously consolidate the state’s writ and provide the former SDF with substantive roles in local and central governance. This outcome would do more than benefit both sides; it also could help clarify options for addressing similar challenges in other parts of a country still recovering from years of brutal civil war. A Series of Negotiations The ceremony on 25 August marked the latest in a series of understandings between the SDF and the central state. The first one, reached in March 2025, was very broadly framed and left many issues unresolved; months of deadlock in talks aimed at fleshing it out gave way to weeks of armed confrontation in early 2026. The subsequent 29 January agreement broke the impasse, reflecting the decisive shift in the balance of power after the government’s rapid military advance. This deal outlined a partial framework for integrating the troops, institutions and lands under SDF control into the Syrian state, but it did not answer key questions concerning the degree and pace of assimilation, among other practical details. Talks continued between the two sides to iron out these issues. At one level, they involved President al-Sharaa, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, Mazloum Abdi and other senior north-eastern figures, who met occasionally to overcome key obstacles. Day-to-day discussions were left to a team appointed by al-Sharaa, working alongside former senior SDF officials named to government positions and other influential figures in the north east. U.S. diplomats, led by presidential envoy Tom Barrack, supported the process, but with a much lighter touch than during the direct mediation in which they engaged throughout much of 2025. Inevitably, these talks reflected the new balance of power that tilted heavily in the central state’s favour after the SDF’s military setback. The organisation nonetheless retained leverage, however diminished: as SDF leaders were well aware, Damascus was eager for them to officially dissolve the group and thus demonstrate their genuine commitment to integration. Weeks of intermittent exchanges centred on two issues in particular: the roles senior north-eastern figures would play in the central government and the scope of Kurdish-language instruction in schools. Kurdish representation at such senior levels of state power is a clear departure from the decades of exclusion and neglect the community endured under Baathist rule. The two sides finally reached a package of understandings on those matters in the hours preceding the SDF’s 25 August dissolution announcement. Mazloum Abdi agreed to become a presidential adviser, while Ilham Ahmad, head of the SDF’s external relations and a central player in the negotiations, assented to taking a seat in the Syrian parliament. These positions are of a lower rank than those informally suggested by SDF leaders, U.S. officials and other intermediaries, who had floated the idea of Abdi serving on Syria’s new national security council and Ahmad assuming a senior foreign ministry post. Nevertheless, they offer Kurdish leaders a foothold in the central government, supplementing key roles already filled by (former) SDF figures in the nascent integrated military and security structures in the north east. These include Sipan Hemo (until January, a leading SDF figure, now serving as assistant minister of defence for the north east) and Mahmoud Khalil Ali (aka “Siamand Afrin”), who previously led the SDF’s Asayesh security forces and is now deputy head of state security forces in the Hassaka governorate. Kurdish representation at such senior levels of state power is a clear departure from the decades of exclusion and neglect the community endured under Baathist rule. The two sides likewise reached a compromise on Kurdish-language education. Under the SDF-aligned administration, Kurdish had been the prevalent language of instruction in most classes offered in Kurdish areas. As the central government assumes responsibility for schools throughout the north east, SDF negotiators had aimed to maintain as much Kurdish-language instruction as possible. At first, Damascus wanted to limit Kurdish-language classes to just two hours per week. In the end, the central government agreed that schools in areas where Kurds form a significant percentage of the population would provide three hours weekly of Kurdish-language instruction and a fourth hour of “activities” in Kurdish. It also consented to having four core subjects – social studies, history, geography and philosophy – offered in Kurdish during the current academic year, albeit not necessarily beyond that. This compromise built on Damascus’s decision in June to recognise diplomas previously issued by the SDF-linked administration. It also expanded on points outlined in a decree issued by al-Sharaa in January – which, in addition to broader commitments on Kurdish rights, acknowledged Kurdish as a national language and permitted elective Kurdish-language courses. Though the August agreement went beyond Damascus’s previous positions, it still fell short of aspirations held by many Syrian Kurds. In subsequent days, Kurdish organisations (including some allied with the SDF) demonstrated in favour of expanded Kurdish instruction. In a nod to those demands, Mazloum Abdi noted in his remarks announcing the SDF’s dissolution that “we will work to implement this decision [on education] in the current year, so that we can build on it in the future”. Gaps Ahead Meanwhile, other files remain subject to further negotiation. The two sides have yet to fully agree on how members of the SDF’s Women’s Protection Units (in Kurdish, Yekîneyên Parastina Jinê , or YPJ) will be incorporated into government forces. Damascus rebuffed SDF proposals to integrate the all-women force into Syria’s nascent post-Assad military, which currently excludes women from combat units. It suggested instead that they be placed under the interior ministry, which in recent months has begun recruiting women throughout the country into police forces. SDF and YPJ leaders have signalled openness to this idea in principle, while pushing to maintain the YPJ’s structural coherence and focus on counter-terrorism , building on its role in combating ISIS. Damascus and Kurdish leaders continued discussing this matter amid their late August meetings, but they have yet to reach an understanding. Beyond these immediate practical gaps lies a more essential divergence that has marked negotiations since early 2025, namely over how centralised each side believes the new Syrian state should be, and thus over how to define integration , particularly in Kurdish population centres. Both concur that the north east should be fully incorporated within state institutions, but they differ on the degree to which former SDF-linked structures, military as well as civilian, should be able to retain their coherence and the extent to which authority would be locally delegated. To date, Damascus has been prepared to live with a light-touch integration of Kurdish entities into the all-important military and security sectors. To date, Damascus has been prepared to live with a light-touch integration of Kurdish entities into the all-important military and security sectors, with SDF and Asayesh forces maintaining much of their structural integrity under the command of senior officers appointed by Damascus. As a result, Kurdish residents’ primary day-to-day interaction with government forces in the north east has been with Kurdish personnel reporting to an integrated chain of command. Such was still the case after the central state sent more of its forces to the region, most recently through the 1 September deployment of additional personnel to Hassaka city. The approach appears to have been largely successful, extending the reach of state sovereignty throughout the north east while keeping public safety in local hands and mitigating concerns among Kurds about how they would fare with non-Kurdish forces. But the written agreements the sides have signed thus far do not clearly define the terms of these arrangements. Nor do they indicate how long the arrangements will stay in place, leaving open the question of whether and to what extent Damascus might push to deepen central authority as time goes by. This ambiguity was a key reason why the SDF repeatedly advocated for solidifying the understandings through some form of constitutional guarantee. Damascus demurred, deferring talks about that demand to forthcoming discussions of Syria’s future constitution. Kurdish leaders have also made clear their intention to press in those discussions for more explicit constitutional linguistic and cultural protections. The timeframe and process for drafting the constitution remain uncertain, as does the mechanism that would allow for input by Kurdish leaders. Addressing Challenges, Clarifying Gains Beyond these gaps, three challenges stand out: returning displaced persons to their homes; managing incidents that threaten to ignite ethnic and political tensions; and addressing the sharp cost-of-living increase that is, at least in part, a by-product of integration. The issue of displaced persons counts among the most sensitive in northern Syria. Both Kurds and Arabs suffered large-scale displacement during the civil war, with tens of thousands of Kurds forced to leave their homes during offensives in which Syrian opposition forces backed by Türkiye seized the district of Afrin (in north-western Syria) and the towns of Ras al-Ayn and Tel Abyadh (in the north east) from Kurdish-led forces allied with the SDF. Thousands of Arab residents also fled during various SDF advances. Some of the resulting demographic changes persist to this day, exacerbating ethnic tensions that for decades were stoked by the forced Arabisation policies of Bashar al-Assad and his father, Hafez. Both Damascus and Kurdish leaders assert that securing the safe return of displaced persons is a priority. Both Damascus and Kurdish leaders assert that securing the safe return of displaced persons is a priority, and they have restated their commitment to that goal at every stage of negotiations. Together, they have achieved significant progress since the 29 January agreement. Between March and July, some 11,000 families returned to Afrin in convoys organised by government officials (including Damascus appointees and former SDF figures) in coordination with a committee representing the displaced. The influx of returnees has helped both restore Afrin’s social fabric and mitigate concerns among senior Kurdish figures who harboured doubts about integration. The government launched a similar cooperative effort to facilitate returns to and around Ras al-Ayn, an ethnically mixed town known in Kurdish as Serê Kaniyê. Yet serious obstacles have emerged of late. On 10 August, armed men attacked the first convoy carrying Kurdish families returning to Ras al-Ayn. As reports of violence spread, demonstrations erupted in Kurdish population centres in the north east, with a number of protesters reportedly attempting to break into central government facilities. Competing narratives of what motivated the attacks are difficult to parse, and no settled account has emerged. Kurdish leaders and government officials worked together to restore calm, with Mazloum Abdi calling for demonstrators to preserve state institutions and government forces announcing the arrest of several Ras al-Ayn assailants. The incident nevertheless underscored the limits of state authority in an area that until 2025 was controlled by poorly disciplined rebel factions, which seized it from the SDF during a Turkish-backed offensive in 2019. Those factions have since been incorporated into state forces, but their assimilation is far from complete. The government suspended returns to Ras al-Ayn town until conditions improve, which will entail addressing property disputes and dampening ethnic tensions in a location awash with guns. Their success in developing a cooperative model notwithstanding, the government and Kurdish leaders face significant challenges in trying to build on the example of Afrin. The returns file is but one example of how local sparks can ignite broader tensions in the north east. On 10 September, Sipan Hazni, a Kurdish former SDF soldier who had recently joined an integrated Syrian army unit, was kidnapped and brutally killed. Purported images of the murder circulated online, along with reports alleging that the killers were Arab tribesmen. As in August, protesters poured into the streets in Kurdish-majority towns and neighbourhoods, and some reportedly attempted to storm government facilities. This time, however, events escalated further in the town of Kobani (known in Arabic as Ayn al-Arab). The interior ministry deployed additional forces to the town, citing altercations that had left security personnel with injuries. Those forces arrested several demonstrators, then attempted to transport some of them from a prison in Kobani to Aleppo – in other words, from a facility still administered by former SDF-aligned personnel to one run by the central government. A prisoner reportedly lit a fire to protest the transfer, and nine detainees perished in the flames. Reactions in each camp underlined the challenges integration faces, but also its potential. Mistrust was evident, particularly in the episode’s early hours. An interior ministry official said some of those arrested were former SDF fighters, implying that elements of the former SDF that oppose integration were fanning unrest. Within SDF circles, the government’s deployment of reinforcements and attempt to transfer Kurdish detainees to facilities outside the north east bolstered concerns about further centralisation of security authority. Yet despite such misgivings, officials from both camps cooperated to quell the disturbance and signalled they would work together to investigate the incidents culminating in the prison fire. Mazloum Abdi’s role was particularly salient: meeting in Kobani with grieving family members and a range of local notables, he addressed concerns about the unrest and the integration process in his new capacity as adviser to President al-Sharaa. The combination of subsidy cuts and surging energy prices has hit the north east hard, with knock-on effects throughout the local economy. Meanwhile, economic conditions in the north east pose another political challenge, as the cost of living in areas previously governed by the SDF-linked administration has risen significantly. Though inflation is occurring throughout Syria, the surge in prices in the north east during recent months has been particularly acute. It has been driven, at least in part, by changes resulting from integration. When the former SDF-linked administration controlled the area’s oil extraction and economic policy, it provided cheap fuel and various subsidies to electricity generators, bakeries and other facilities, as well as to the vital agricultural sector. But as Damascus extended its writ, it scaled back these benefits, in keeping with its overall determination to maintain fiscal discipline. The combination of subsidy cuts and surging energy prices has hit the north east hard, with knock-on effects throughout the local economy. A steep hike in fuel prices announced by the government on 13 September exacerbated this dynamic, sparking protests in and beyond the north east. Insofar as north-eastern residents link the ensuing financial pain to integration, their faith in the process is fading. As fears resulting from the January military confrontation subside, Kurds in particular are liable to assess integration in terms of its practical impact. They have much to welcome: Kurds now enjoy legal recognition and state institutional roles that were hard to imagine under the previous regime, and the shift from SDF to state governance has eased some of their hardships, including difficulties with their educational diplomas, which previously were not recognised anywhere outside the north east. But, for now at least, the increased cost of living is undermining support among many who otherwise see integration’s benefits and sharpening grievances among those who oppose it. Eyes on the Prize The progress of integration to date is a testament to the foresight of the two sides’ respective leaders. But they need to remain focused on the significant challenges that lie ahead. The stakes are high and the payoff for further progress potentially great. Whereas any setback could have dangerous ramifications for the area’s stability, success could highlight constructive options for addressing governance and integration elsewhere – particularly in southern Syria, where the Druze-majority governorate of Suweida remains outside government control. While the local and geopolitical circumstances differ, the factors that will likely make or break integration in the north east would also be critical to an integration process in Suweida: incorporating local forces to lead in providing day-to-day security; ensuring that the area is well-represented in central government structures; and delivering clear economic gains and better services to the population. Having accomplished several of its priorities – notably extending the state’s institutions and command throughout the north east – Damascus ought to now focus on demonstrating the concrete benefits of integration. The more it is seen to improve security, governance and quality of life for Syrians in the north east, the more credibility integration will attain, including among those who remain understandably apprehensive of central state power after decades of suffering under the Assads. To that end, Damascus should clarify that the SDF’s former Asayesh personnel will form the long-term core of local security forces. It should also ensure that leaders such as Mazloum Abdi and Ilham Ahmad can play substantive, visible policymaking roles, including in drafting a new constitution – progress on which remains essential to Syria’s broader post-Assad transition. Mitigating economic pain in the north east will prove challenging in light of Syria’s fiscal constraints, but Damascus could discuss prospects for external aid to support integration with the U.S., as well as with European and Gulf Arab states. With the SDF now dissolved and several of its leading figures serving as senior government officials, integration may play out less as a negotiation between two parties and more as a mix of bargaining and collaboration among elements of the state. This shift arguably is already well under way locally, as illustrated by how the two camps have worked together to ease displaced persons’ return and to restore calm when tensions have boiled over. If Damascus aims to turn the north east’s integration into a model, building on that cooperation – including at the national level – would be an important way to strengthen its appeal. Iran: Ongoing Unlawful Execution Campaign Against Protesters. Click to expand Image A person's mouth covered with tape bearing a message “no to executions” in Iran, in Paris in France, January 31, 2026. © 2026 Daniel Perron/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images Within a span of only five months, between March 18 and the end of August 2026, Iran’s authorities announced the executions of 29 people in connection with recent protests. These executions were unlawful and in violation of international human rights law. Several protesters executed were teenagers aged 18 and 19. Scores more remain at imminent risk of execution. Some executions have been carried out in public to further instill fear, marking a significant escalation. Executions have followed grossly unfair and summary proceedings, ranging in protest-related cases from just over five weeks to less than eight months from arrest to execution. In most cases, no allegations of killings have been made and protesters have been convicted of vague national security charges and executed for acts such as allegedly damaging public property, throwing stones, or breaking into government buildings. Urgent and coordinated diplomatic action by UN member states is needed, including to encourage the use of measures such as universal jurisdiction to hold officials responsible for serious international crimes, including torture and enforced disappearances, to account. (Beirut) – Iranian authorities are unlawfully executing protesters and political dissidents on a weekly basis, a relentless attack on the right to life, Human Rights Watch and the Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran said today. Between March 18 and end of August 2026, authorities arbitrarily executed at least 59 men on politically motivated and vague national security charges following grossly unfair trials. They include at least 29 arrested in connection with December 2025-January 2026 protests and at least 3 reportedly arrested in connection with the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom protests. Several were teenagers aged 18 or 19 and many others in their early 20s. Five were executed in public, violating the absolute prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment. “Day after day, Iran’s authorities are sending protesters, including teenagers, to the gallows based on torture-tainted ‘confessions’ and following grossly unfair proceedings that are too short to establish a defendant’s guilt even for a minor offense, let alone for capital charges,” said Bahar Saba, senior Iran researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities’ message is clearly that protests will be met with brutality, whether through bullets on the streets or public executions following sham trials.” Human Rights Watch and the Boroumand Center reviewed evidence pertaining to the cases of individuals executed between March 18 and the end of August 2026 as well as people under death sentences or at risk of receiving the death penalty in connection with recent protests. The organizations interviewed 12 individuals, including human rights defenders, journalists, lawyers, former cellmates, and other informed sources. Researchers also examined audio messages from detainees, several audio recordings and transcripts of interviews by human rights defenders that were shared with the organizations, as well as official statements and execution announcements, including by the judiciary’s official news agency, state media reports, human rights organizations’ reporting, and court verdicts in three capital cases. The organizations also reviewed several coerced “confession” videos of individuals later executed that were broadcast on state media. Summary proceedings, torture-tainted “confessions,” and public executions have been the hallmark of the authorities’ weaponization of the death penalty in the aftermath of January 2026 massacres of protesters to instill fear and deter further public dissent, the groups said. The vast majority of protesters have been executed within only six months of their arrest, denying them adequate time to prepare a defense. Saleh Mohammadi, 19, a wrestling champion, was arbitrarily executed about five weeks after his arrest. Amir Hossein Hatami, 18, was arbitrarily executed 84 days after his arrest. Sasan Azadvar Jonaqani, 21, a karate champion, was arrested, convicted, and arbitrarily executed in under four months for acts such as allegedly breaking windows of a police bus with stones and a baton. Capital charges in 16 of the 29 cases did not involve any allegations of killing, let alone intentional killing that international human rights law limits the application of capital punishment to. Under international law, the death penalty is legally exceptional and may be applied, if at all, in the states that have retained it, for the “most serious crimes,” limited to intentional killing only and under the strictest limitations and safeguards. Human Rights Watch and the Boroumand Center oppose the death penalty in all cases without exception, regardless of the nature of the crime, as the ultimate cruel, inhuman, and degrading punishment. Young protesters have been executed for allegedly setting fire to buildings and vehicles; making, possessing, and using Molotov cocktails; and entering and destroying public and government buildings. In at least 10 of the remaining 13 cases, the state raised allegations of involvement in killings or fatal incidents but did not charge defendants with murder. Defendants were solely convicted of vaguely worded crimes, such as “waging war against God” and “corruption on earth.” Authorities have used these vague offenses to sentence people, including groups, to death for alleged acts such as incitement to violence, nonfatal assault, or possession of weapons without establishing their actual role in any killing. In several cases, authorities relied on the charge of “operational action on behalf of hostile states,” a capital offense introduced under a 2025 law titled: “Intensifying Punishments for Spies and Collaborators with the Zionist Regime and Hostile States.” “At least eight protesters were convicted under the vaguely worded 2025 Espionage Law, which broadened punishable conduct and cut procedural deadlines,” said Roya Boroumand, executive director of the Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran. “Originally introduced after the nationwide protests of late 2019 and early 2020, the law has become a fast-tracked mechanism for sentencing protesters to death without evidence of espionage or cooperation with a hostile state and a chilling message to those who might expose how these convictions were obtained.” The organizations documented patterns of denial of access to independent legal counsel of one’s choice and torture and ill-treatment, including beatings, mock executions, and threats of rape. Defendants were sentenced by courts that fundamentally lack independence and impartiality. This includes courts’ systematic use of “confessions” extracted under torture and unsubstantiated reports by security and intelligence bodies as evidence. Scores of other protesters and political dissidents, including women, children, and several people whose co-defendants have already been executed, remain at imminent risk of execution. On July 28, 2026, Amnesty International reported that it had identified 60 people, including 3 children, at risk of execution in connection with protests. The Volunteer Committee to Follow-Up on the Situation of Detainees, a network of Iranian activists in exile, has published the names of over 60 people sentenced to death as of August 14. According to another organization, Iran Human Rights, over 70 protesters are at risk of execution in Isfahan Prison alone. The number of protesters and dissidents at risk of execution is believed to be much higher. Many cases have gone unreported due to internet shutdowns and a well-founded fear of state reprisals. A July official directive by the Ministry of Intelligence, issued under the 2025 Espionage Law, designated hundreds of media outlets, human rights organizations, and activists as “enemies,” criminalizing any contact with them. This has exacerbated the climate of fear, further forcing relatives of victims to remain silent when advocacy and international scrutiny could help save the lives of those on death row, the groups said. Opposition to the death penalty and unlawful execution of protesters is itself treated as “criminal” conduct. On July 30, Tehran’s prosecutor announced that criminal cases had been opened against several people who had expressed their opposition to executions. Authorities have systematically smeared and vilified protesters, including those arbitrarily executed, by labelling them as the “ground troops of a US-Israeli coup” and repeatedly blaming them for “providing a fertile ground and an excuse” for the military strikes against Iran in February. The sharp increase in political executions is taking place against the backdrop of a very significant rise in executions in Iran. The Boroumand Center recorded at least 2,113 in 2025, the highest annual known number since the late 1980s. United Nations member states should urgently press Iran’s authorities to halt all executions and establish a moratorium leading to abolition of the death penalty, Human Rights Watch and the Boroumand Center said. UN bodies and experts and human rights organizations have found that systematic, structural, and historical impunity in Iran for those responsible for violations and crimes under international law, including judicial and prosecutorial officials, remain a key driver of atrocities in the country. In its reports since 2024, the UN Fact-Finding Mission on Iran has found that “judges issuing death sentences relied on torture-tainted evidence and presided over trials marred by serious fair trial violations” and, in that context, may be responsible for serious crimes under international law. Given the impunity in Iran, judicial authorities in other countries should carry out investigations under the principle of universal jurisdiction with a view toward holding Iranian officials suspected of responsibility for serious international crimes to account. Where sufficient evidence exists, states should prosecute these crimes in accordance with national laws. States that provide for structural investigations—that is, investigations that examine patterns of violations which can then be linked to specific cases for individual prosecutions—should collect and preserve evidence in connection with serious international crimes committed in Iran to facilitate future criminal proceedings. Unlawful and Arbitrary Executions in Iran Under international human rights law, deprivation of life is, as a rule, arbitrary if it is inconsistent with international law or domestic law. International human rights law imposes severe restrictions on the use of the death penalty in countries that have retained it. The imposition of the death penalty in a manner that is contrary to provisions of the International Covenant on Civil or Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Iran is a state party, and without strict adherence with safeguards and restrictions imposed on the use of the death penalty would render executions arbitrary. For instance, executions carried out on the basis of death sentences issued for offenses that do not meet the threshold of the “most serious crimes” as well as vaguely worded offenses that breach the principle of legality are arbitrary deprivations of life. Similarly, violations of fair trial guarantees provided under article 14 of the ICCPR also render executions arbitrary in nature according to the UN Human Rights Committee. This includes the use of forced confessions, denial of access to independent lawyers of one’s choosing, denial of the right to presumption of innocence, denial of the right to seek pardons and commutations of a death sentence, and a lack of independence or impartiality of the trial or the court. While Human Rights Watch and the Boroumand Center primarily focused on 29 execution cases connected with recent protests, the organizations found similar patterns of gross violations of international human rights law in other cases. In at least 58 out of the 59 cases, people had conviction on the basis of vaguely worded charges such as “waging war against God,” “corruption on earth” “armed rebellion,” espionage, and “operational activity on behalf of hostile states.” These charges fall under the jurisdiction of revolutionary courts, which lack independence and impartiality and are responsible for the majority of death sentences in Iran. According to official reports, in two cases, defendants were convicted of both murder and vaguely worded offenses in connection with the same acts. In most cases, authorities have not made any allegations of involvement in killings. Additionally, based on Iran’s domestic laws, individuals have been denied access to lawyers of their choosing during the preliminary investigations. In 2021, the then UN Special Rapporteur on Iran stated: “The entrenched flaws in law and in the administration of the death penalty in Iran mean that most, if not all, executions are an arbitrary deprivation of life.” Executions for Vague Charges, Alleged Property Damage Between March 18 and the end of August 2026, authorities announced the executions of 29 people in connection with recent protests, almost all on the basis of vaguely worded laws that contravene the principle of legality, given that persons could not predict that an act would amount to a crime. The charges against 16 involved no allegations of killing, let alone intentional killing. In one of the remaining cases, a protester was broadly accused of having led “riots that resulted” in the deaths of members of security forces. Under international human rights law, the death penalty is legally exceptional and may be applied, if at all, in the states that have retained it, for the “most serious crimes,” limited to intentional killing only and under the strictest limitations and safeguards. Contrary to international law, Iranian authorities have executed protesters for acts such as blocking streets, damaging public property, and conduct deemed collaboration with “hostile states” as stipulated under the 2025 Espionage Law, which was first introduced in parliament in 2020 and fast-tracked for adoption following the June 2025 Israel-Iran armed conflict. None of these charges reach the threshold of “the most serious crimes.” On April 30, 2026, Branch 1 of Revolutionary Court in Isfahan arbitrarily executed Sasan Azadvar Jonaqani, 21, for “waging war against God.” According to excerpts from the verdict, published by the judiciary’s news agency, Mizan, the government did not allege that Azadvar had killed anyone. Instead, he was accused of “actively participating in riots,” “attacking and throwing stones at security forces,” causing damage to private vehicles, and “inciting and encouraging people at the scene to riot and [cause] unrest.” Erfan Kiani, arbitrarily executed on April 25, was convicted of “waging war against God” for alleged involvement in similar acts. Mizan reported he was accused of throwing stones and a Molotov cocktail toward security forces, acts of vandalism such as destruction of traffic cameras, possession of a machete, and obstructing a street. On June 1, authorities arbitrarily executed Ashkan Maleki and Mehrdad Mohammadinia, from Iran’s oppressed Kurdish minority, in Alborz province. Mizan reported that Branch 15 of the Revolutionary Court in Tehran had sentenced them to death for “participating in operational action against national security on behalf of the Zionist regime and the hostile state of US and hostile groups” as well as “entering sacred religious buildings with intent to destroy and set fire to public and private property… to confront the sacred system of the Islamic Republic during war.” Mizan reported they were convicted and sentenced to death under the 2025 Espionage Law, based on “confessions” in detention and reports by intelligence and security bodies. A co-defendant, Arman Marefati, also Kurdish, is at imminent risk of execution. On July 22, authorities announced that Mehdi Khanaki had been executed. Mizanreported that a revolutionary court in Karaj, Alborz province, convicted him of “operational action in favor of the Zionist regime, the United States, and hostile groups” and of “manufacturing, procuring, and possessing military weapons and ammunition and using them” and sentenced him to death under the Espionage Law. The authorities accused Khanaki of membership in an unnamed “terrorist group” and of taking part in the “US-Zionist coup,” a term the government often uses in reference to the December 2025-January 2026 protests. Mizan reported that according to weapons experts, the weapons allegedly seized from his residence had been discharged during “the time period of the riots of December/January.” The authorities did not tie the alleged use of the weapons to any specific incidents or accuse Khanaki of any involvement in killings. Other protesters remain on death row and at risk of execution for alleged acts that did not involve intentional killing. Benyamin Naghdi, 26, a mixed martial arts fighter and kickboxer, is at imminent risk of execution after Branch 41 of the Supreme Court upheld his death sentence in July. Branch 1 of the Revolutionary Court in Shiraz sentenced him to death for “corruption on earth” for allegedly using a fire extinguisher as a makeshift flamethrower against security forces passing by on motorcycles during protests in Shiraz, Fars province, on January 3. In a media interview with a domestic outlet, Naghdi’s lawyer, Mostafa Nili, said that Naghdi had initially been charged with attempted murder. But after preliminary investigations, he was indicted for “waging war against God,” “membership in groups disrupting national security,” “gathering and colluding to commit crimes against national security,” and “propaganda against the system.” Prosecutors dropped charges pertaining to inflicting bodily injury on security forces and possession of a cold weapon, Nili said, but judges ruled that the charges against his client collectively amounted to “corruption on earth.” Nili said that no one was injured during the incident. On July 15, the authorities arbitrarily executed Mohammad Amini Dehaghani, arrested in connection with protests in Isfahan province after convicting him of “waging war against God” and “corruption on Earth.” Mizanreported he was accused of blocking roads, setting fire to the Dehaghan governor’s office with a Molotov cocktail, throwing a Molotov cocktail at a local police station and inciting others to attack the police station on January 9, and “requesting [others to give him] a Kalashnikov rifle to fire.” He was further accused of “propaganda against the system,” “disturbing the public opinion and the society’s psychological security,” and “communicating with opposition channels.” Mizan reported he was convicted based on his “confessions” and CCTV footage that allegedly showed him participating in the attack on the governor’s office. The authorities did not report any deaths or injuries in the alleged attack. Official court statements and execution announcements show that at least eight men executed in connection with recent protests were convicted under the 2025 Espionage Law. Iran’s laws already make a wide range of conduct punishable by death, including free expression, which is protected under international human rights law. The Espionage Law has further expanded the scope of capital punishment, imposing the death penalty for vaguely worded offenses pertaining to collaboration and cooperation with “hostile states” and long prison terms for acts such as “sending footage, images, or information to [media] networks, citizen journalists, or online foreign [social media] pages where [such acts] contravene national security.” The law also provides for expedited proceedings by special branches of revolutionary courts, including cutting the appeal time from 20 days to 10. Failure to Establish Individual Guilt, Denial of Right to Effective Defense Prosecutorial and judicial officials have violated the rights of those convicted of capital offenses, including of the presumption of innocence, and in cases where Human Rights Watch and the Boroumand Center were able to obtain information, officials failed to clearly establish the individual guilt of those convicted, including in cases where authorities accuse defendants of involvement in killings. Under General Comment 36 of the UN Human Rights Committee, the execution of a sentenced person whose guilt has not been established beyond reasonable doubt constitutes an arbitrary deprivation of life.
